A simple one today! No breaking changes, just two small things.

 We have a bigger release in the works probably for next Thursday.

 For today:

 Added a small temporary flag on describeServer for determining if you’re talking to a spaces-alpha compatible PDS ( Impl / Forum Thread )

 Tightening up space repo lifecycle. In the code, specifically ensuring that the space exists before posting in a repo where the authorities are the same ( Impl / Spec )

We just cut another spaces alpha release today!

 This is the biggest yet, there are multiple breaking changes across core protocol pieces. This is likely the last/only release of this size. Though we are planning to do a smaller (tho still substantial & backwards-incompatible) release next Thursday. The hope is that that will be the last breaking alpha release. Then we can use November to do final shakeout, before moving to beta at the end of the month.

 I expect this rollout to be somewhat disruptive. We have updated the hosted spaces alpha PDS, the Docker image at ghcr.io/bluesky-social/atproto:pds-spaces-alpha and the relevant npm packages. For folks running their own PDS, this release includes database migrations on both the account manager DB & the actor store DBs as well as adding a new per-account key which will require a DID doc update for each account (see below).

 Like last time, we’ve put together a prompt that you can give your coding agent to handle the migration.

 To summarize the changes:

 Shared secret commits. This is the biggest change. Space repo commit HMACs are now done using a negotiated shared secret between a syncer and a repo host. This requires introducing a new #atproto_kem key for each user and commit MACs are sent in HTTP headers. We also tweaked some field names in the commit such as hash → data . Rationale is in this thread . ( Implementation / Proposal )

 STAR files. getRepo now returns a STAR archive instead of a CAR file. Thanks @bad-example.com ! ( Implementation / Proposal )

 Public spaces. Spaces can issue credentials without a delegation token. As part of this, we moved the delegation token & HTTP signature key material to the request body of getSpaceCredential (instead of headers). Also tweaked the authorization scheme name for consistency. ( Implementation / Proposal )

 Simpler DID doc keys. To avoid some complexity, we ditched the new space host signing key & service endpoint in DID docs. Space authorities resolve like any other account: #atproto_pds is the space host and #atproto signs credentials. ( Implementation / Proposal )

 Reliable space deletion. Space authorities retry notifySpaceDeleted until it’s delivered or the syncer’s registration expires. This mirrors the robust delivery of write notifications from repo host to space host. ( Implementation / Proposal )

 All of the spec changes for this release are combined in proposals#125 .

 We also updated the version of Node in the published Docker image in response to the eMudhra CA compromise.

 A note on KEM keys: every account with space repos now needs an #atproto_kem key in its DID doc. New accounts get one automatically. For existing accounts, the PDS runs a one-time background backfill on startup that generates the key & publishes an update PLC. This should Just Work ! However, it touches every account on the PDS, so self-hosters should expect a PLC update and an #identity event per account. If your account uses did:web, or your PDS can’t update your PLC doc, you’ll need to add the key yourself ( getRecommendedDidCredentials returns it). Until an account’s key is published, its space repos can’t be synced. Account migration tools also need to carry atproto_kem through from getRecommendedDidCredentials , since submitPlcOperation now checks it.

 As always, please let me know if you have feedback or if you run into bugs or sharp edges!

value.title: Space Membership Checks
value.textContent:
I’m working through the technical details and want to confirm my understanding.

 Currently it is not possible for a feed server to independently verify the membership of an identity to a space with formal protocol channels or mechanics.

 did:plc:foo authenticates with ExampleApp https://example.app/ 

 ExampleApp creates service-auth token for getFeedSkeleton on behalf of did:plc:foo to FeedServer https://feeds.app/ 

 ExampleApp requests getFeedSkeleton from FeedServer https://feeds.app/ for did:plc:foo with the service-auth token

 FeedServer has no ability to determine if did:plc:foo is a member of space did:plc:bar/com.example.space/baz

 For FeedServer to know if did:plc:foo is a member of space did:plc:bar/com.example.space/baz, one of these must happen:

 The feed server has its own auth where it gets an identity access token and can mint a space credential to test authentication. This sucks for a lot of reasons.

 The AppView sends additional data* that must be trusted that says the requesting identity has access to the space. This sucks for different reasons.

 The space must be configured with a membership-app that can be queried by FeedServer directly. This sucks also sucks for different reasons.

 I propose that the checkUserAccess be implemented by the space host and can be queried with service authentication by members of the space. That would allow FeedServer to install a “service account” as a member of the space that could then make service auth requests as needed.

value.title: Proposal: seal and unseal operations for did:plc
value.textContent:
I recently wrote about account recovery and password reset using rotation keys , and now I’d like to propose another method to strengthen identity document security.

 It started with the question “what can a did-method-plc identity do moments after its holder realizes something is wrong?” Today the answer is “undo one thing, then hope.” This is a proposal for two new operation types, plc_seal and plc_unseal, that let an account holder use a high-authority rotation key to switch off the keys below it temporarily.

 Problem

 Rotation keys in did-method-plc identities are an ordered list, and that order is critical to the security model. A key earlier in the list can nullify an operation signed by a key later in the list, as long as it does so within 72 hours by forking from the operation before the bad one. This is a good mechanism, and it’s why the standard advice for anyone who cares about their identity is to put a key they control ahead of the key their PDS holds.

 What the 72-hour window gives you is the ability to react and undo (not negate) PLC operations. It does not give you the ability to invoke any immediate preventative measures.

 This is the scenario that worries me the most: An account has rotation keys [A, B], where A is a key the holder keeps offline, and B is the PDS operator’s key. An attacker gets into the holder’s email, and from there into the account, and uses the PDS’s own com.atproto.identity.requestPlcOperationSignature and signPlcOperation flow. The PDS does exactly what it is supposed to do: it emails a token, the attacker pastes it back, and the PDS signs a PLC operation with B that points the identity at a different host. The holder notices, pulls out A, forks past the attacker’s operation, and restores the correct state. Good. Then the attacker requests another signature. The PDS signs again with B. PLC has nothing that lets the holder say, “B is not allowed to sign right now,” so this repeats until the holder wins the race to reset the email and password, and every round gives the holder a fresh 72-hour window to be awake.

 The one lever the holder does have is removing B from rotationKeys. That stops the attacker and also stops the PDS from doing its job: no handle changes, no signing key rotation, no migration assistance, and no bulk DID document updates like the ones the Spaces work will need ( #atproto_space and #atproto_space_host ). It is a permanent fix for a temporary problem, and it is reversible only if the holder adds the key back later and remembers to.

 Design

 I landed on “seal” and “unseal” actions. A seal names a specific rotation key in the rotation key list. While the seal is in effect, the directory accepts operations signed by that key or the keys listed before it, and rejects operations signed by any keys listed after it. For example, given the keys [A, B, C, D], sealing at B would allow operations signed by A and B, but not C and D.

 A seal restricts who may sign, not what they may write. Authorized keys can still change fields, including removing an excluded key that turns out to be compromised. Put differently, the seal is not a freeze on the DID document, but it is a constraint on who can sign PLC operations.

 The seal key is named by its did:key value, not by its index. 

 Every seal has a duration, and the duration is bounded. This is measured from the directory’s own createdAt timestamp for the seal PLC operation. Expiry is a safety net for critical failure: sealing a key and then losing it. The cost of the bound is that the expiry time is public, so an attacker who still holds the operator key knows exactly when to try again. I have mixed feelings about this, but kept the duration since a permanent lockout from a lost key seemed worse than a known retry date.

 Seal state is derived from the operation log. There is no directory-side flag. The sealed check involves walking the valid operations and computing the last plc_seal not followed by a plc_unseal is the active seal where createdAt + sealDuration is still in the future. Mirrors recompute it the same way, and anyone auditing the log would catch a directory that accepted an operation in violation of a seal, which fits the existing trust model.

 Seal and unseal operations carry the full identity state, like plc_operation does. This means a single plc_seal with prev set to the fork point before the attacker’s operation both nullifies that operation and installs the seal in one acceptance decision. There is no window between recovery and lockdown for the attacker to slip another operation into. It is the strongest protection the account holder has against the scenario described above.

 A seal never removes authority from a key above its signer. A key can seal at its own level or at the level of a key below it, and it always stays authorized under the seal it creates. Keys above the seal’s signer can nullify the seal within 72 hours, unseal at any time, or re-seal at a different key. So an attacker who holds B can at most lock out C and D, which B could already do damage with, and A is unaffected.

 Solution

 PLC Operations

 A plc_seal is a plc_operation with two additional fields and a different type. sealKey is the did:key of the key to seal at, and sealDuration is an integer number of seconds. Both are signed over like everything else, and sealDuration is a plain unsigned integer in DAG-CBOR.

 {
 "type": "plc_seal",
 "rotationKeys": [
 "did:key:zQ3shUserRecoveryKeyA",
 "did:key:zQ3shOperatorKeyB",
 "did:key:zQ3shOperatorKeyC"
 ],
 "verificationMethods": {
 "atproto": "did:key:zQ3shAtprotoSigningKey"
 },
 "alsoKnownAs": ["at://alice.example.com"],
 "services": {
 "atproto_pds": {
 "type": "AtprotoPersonalDataServer",
 "endpoint": "https://pds.example.com"
 }
 },
 "sealKey": "did:key:zQ3shUserRecoveryKeyA",
 "sealDuration": 604800,
 "prev": "bafyreigq3zpkj5n2ax3m7ubyqdyfcc2lhw4vbhe4b3l4qkq5ssdvmrlbka",
 "sig": "<base64url signature by key A>"
}

 A plc_unseal is the same shape without the two seal fields. It must be signed by the seal key or a key above it, and it is only valid while a seal is in effect.

 {
 "type": "plc_unseal",
 "rotationKeys": ["<same as above>"],
 "verificationMethods": { "atproto": "<same>" },
 "alsoKnownAs": ["at://alice.example.com"],
 "services": { "atproto_pds": "<same>" },
 "prev": "bafyreih6v4m2ykc5o7s2nq3ugxw2l3pbz7rj5kzq7c4wyf2v3xg6ad3xqe",
 "sig": "<base64url signature by key A>"
}

 Constraints On Seal

 A plc_seal is valid when

 The prev value points to an existing valid operation (a seal is never a genesis op)

 The sealKey value appears in the operation’s own rotationKeys

 At least one rotation key is listed after sealKey, so the DID has at least two keys and the seal excludes at least one of them.

 The sealDuration value is an integer between 3600 and 2592000, inclusive.

 The key that signed the operation, if it appears in the operation’s rotationKeys, is listed at or before sealKey

 The last rule keeps a key from locking itself out. A seal excludes every key listed after sealKey, so a seal whose signer sits after sealKey would exclude the very key that placed it. With keys [A, B, C, D], a seal signed by C can name C as the seal key but cannot name A or B; a seal signed by A can name any of A, B, or C. The check runs against the operation’s own rotationKeys rather than the previous state’s, because a seal carries full state and can reorder keys in the same step. If B signs a seal with rotationKeys: [A, C, B] and sealKey: C, then B has moved itself below the seal key and the operation is rejected. A signer that removes itself from rotationKeys entirely is not subject to this rule, since there is nothing left to exclude.

 If the DID is already sealed when the seal operation arrives, the operation is also subject to the rules in the next section: its signer has to be authorized under the existing seal. On acceptance, it replaces the active seal, and the new seal key and duration apply from the new operation’s createdAt.

 Constraints On Unseal

 A plc_unseal is valid when

 The prev field value points to an existing valid operation (an unseal is never a genesis op)

 The DID is sealed at prev as of the time of submission, meaning a seal operation is active in the chain ending at prev,and its sealDuration has not elapsed.

 The key that signed the operation is authorized under that seal: it appears in prev’s rotationKeys at or before the seal key.

 An unseal is subject to the same seal rule as every other operation on a sealed DID, and nothing more. Its signer has to be one of the keys the seal left standing; there is no separate unseal authority. With keys [A, B, C, D] sealed at B, either A or Bcan unseal, and C or D cannot. The system rejects an unseal submitted when no seal is active, since there is nothing to lift. An unseal submitted after the seal has expired is rejected for the same reason, so a client that wants to lift a seal should check /data first rather than assuming one is still in effect.

 Because an unseal carries full state, it may change rotationKeys, verificationMethods, alsoKnownAs, and services in the same step. An unseal may remove the seal key, since the seal no longer applies once the operation is accepted. An unseal is nullifiable under the ordinary recovery rules: a key of higher authority than the unseal’s signer can fork past it within 72 hours, which puts the DID back under the seal that was in effect before the unseal.

 Operation Evaluation

 When an operation of any type arrives, the directory works out whether the DID is sealed at the operation’s prev, as of the timestamp it is about to assign. Evaluating at prev rather than at the head of the log is deliberate, and I’ll explain why in a moment. If it is sealed, three rules apply on top of signature checking and the existing recovery rules.

 The signing key has to be authorized: it appears in prev’s rotationKeys at an index less than or equal to the seal key’s index there. This applies to regular ops, seals, unseals, and tombstones.

 A plc_operation keeps the seal key in its rotationKeys. It can add, remove, and reorder other keys freely. Changing the seal key is what plc_seal is for; lifting it is what plc_unseal is for.

 A plc_operation does not demote its own signer below the seal key. That protects against an authorized key accidentally locking itself out.

 Seal state is evaluated at prev because a recovery operation has to be judged by the seal that was in effect at its fork point. If we judged it against the head of the log, then B could seal at B, remove A with an ordinary operation, and A’s 72-hour fork would be rejected because A is no longer in the head’s rotationKeys. Evaluating at the fork point, where A is still listed, keeps the existing recovery guarantee intact.

 That alone opens a different hole. Suppose D signs an operation, B seals at B on top of it, and C then forks from before D’s op. Under the current recovery rule, C only has to outrank the key that started the branch, which is D, so C would nullify B’s seal along with everything else and escape it. The fix is one extra condition on recovery: an operation that would nullify a plc_seal has to be signed by a key that outranks the seal’s signer at the fork point. With that in place, A can still fork behind the seal and C cannot.

 I checked this pair of rules against the cases I could think of: remove-then-reseal, unseal-remove-reseal, a seal that itself removes a higher key, and a seal whose signer was added after the fork point. It held up in each, but this is the part of the proposal most worth an adversarial read.

 API Changes

 GET /:did/data gains a seal object while sealed, and nothing when not. It carries only what cannot be derived from the rest of the response: the seal key, the CID of the seal operation (whose createdAt is in the audit log), and the expiry. The DID document itself is unchanged, since rotation keys are already an internal detail and seal state means nothing without them.

 {
 "did": "did:plc:ewvi7nxzyoun6zhxrhs64oiz",
 "rotationKeys": ["...A", "...B", "...C"],
 "verificationMethods": { "atproto": "..." },
 "alsoKnownAs": ["at://alice.example.com"],
 "services": { "atproto_pds": { "...": "..." } },
 "seal": {
 "key": "did:key:zQ3shUserRecoveryKeyA",
 "cid": "bafyreih6v4m2ykc5o7s2nq3ugxw2l3pbz7rj5kzq7c4wyf2v3xg6ad3xqe",
 "expiresAt": "2026-10-26T14:02:11.512Z"
 }
}

 The audit log needs no schema change. Seal and unseal ops show up as ordinary entries with cid, createdAt, and nullified, and auditors recompute the seal state from them.

 The Attack, But With Seals

 Back to [A, B] plus the email flow. The attacker’s operation lands, signed by B. The holder signs one plc_seal with A: prev is the last good operation, the state fields restore the right PDS and signing key, sealKey is A, and sealDuration is a week. The directory accepts it, nullifies the attacker’s op, and seals the DID. The attacker requests another signature. The PDS can still sign with B, but the directory rejects the result because B is excluded. The holder resets the email and password at their own pace and either unseals with A or lets the week run out.

 A rejected submission looks like any other invalid operation today: a 400 with a message. I’d propose adding a stable errorcode alongside it so PDS software can tell a seal rejection apart from a bad signature:

 {
 "error": "SealedOperationRejected",
 "message": "DID is sealed with rotation key X until 2026-10-26T14:02:11.512Z"
}

 PDS Operator Cost

 While sealed at a holder-controlled key, the PDS’s key is excluded, so the PDS cannot rotate the signing key, change a service endpoint, update the handle, help with a migration, or apply protocol-wide DID document changes. That is the point of the feature, and it is also why most accounts shouldn’t use it regularly. A PDS that hits SealedOperationRejectedshould surface an IdentitySealed error to the user with the expiry, remind them that the account is sealed, and retry after it. requestPlcOperationSignature should check /data first and refuse to send an email token at all when the PDS’s key is excluded, which during an attack is the behavior you want anyway. Migration is still possible while sealed; the holder signs the migration op with the seal key, keeps the seal key in rotationKeys, and the new operator’s key sits below it until the seal lifts.

 Closing

 This is not a backward-compatible change in the quiet sense. The reference implementation and production PLC Directory reject unspecified fields, the TypeScript export schemas look like a closed union on type, and go-didplc and my Rust crates parse only the shapes they know about. Submitting a seal today fails safely-ish. Libraries that read, parse, and validate the audit logs will need updates to support these new data structures, plus the behavior and constraints they introduce.

 I’m not entirely sure what the next steps are. I want to incorporate feedback into a proposal to the PLC organization. Attached are the patch to the specification document and a rendered version of the specification document:

 did-plc.md 

 did-plc.patch

This is a long proposal (a lot to read). It feels like a lot of complexity to work around a bad account security situation: if you don’t have control of your PDS account, and your PDS has a rotation key, then you have a big problem and you can’t trust anything your PDS might do with any atproto resources: public repo contents, service proxying, etc.

 It feels like you’d probably want to be able to lock down the PDS account immediately: halt any PDS-assisted identity updates, terminate all OAuth client sessions, stop doing service proxying, and maybe put the account in a deactivated state. That is all disruptive, but this is a disruptive scenario.

 If you had control of the PLC identity and wanted to take action there, it would feel simplest to me to remove the PDS-controlled rotation key, and possibly also the #atproto signing key and #atproto_pds service endpoint. If you can’t trust the PDS to be acting on your identity’s behalf, I don’t think those should be in the DID document at all. That is again quite disruptive, but it is a disruptive situation.

Yeah, it is complex machinery that is intended to be used in a worst cast scenario. Some follow up thoughts that didn’t make it into the original post:

 Absolutely all of it hinges on the idea that accounts have rotation keys that they control and that is not currently common or typical. I don’t have any immediate states, but I’d guess that less than 1% of active atmospheric identities have a rotation key on their DID document that isn’t set by their PDS operator.

 I would also use this as a travel scenario. If I have keys [A, B, C] where C is from my PDS, B is a hardware key, and A is an offline key, and then I want to travel abroad where B could be stolen or confiscated, maybe I preemptively seal my document with A for the duration of the trip. Gives 1password and Apple / Google Enhanced Security vibes.

How about removing plc did document editing /signing completely from the PDS and move it to a native identity app (wallet) with the rotation key in a hardware enclave and a top level rotation key stored offline.

 The only thing a PDS does then is submitting (the wallet can verify a submission out of band ) the did document to PLC directory and emitting an identity event

value.title: Extending Lexicons: sidecar records patterns and typed extensions
value.textContent:
Hello! I wanted to start a general discussion about Lexicon extensions and sidecar records, brought up by the need to connect records, web pages and apps .

 For reference:

 A sidecar record is a special-by-convention (yet regular) record that holds additional information about another one. For example, a sidecar record for an app.bsky.feed.post record may hold additional information about who’s allowed to reply to the post.

 The mechanism is extensively used but AFAIK not fully documented. So to put everyone on the same page, I did some research on patterns out there and some thinking on pros/cons. I tried to be objective, but feel free to point out what I may be missing 

 These patterns can overlap, and some examples may be better described as related records than sidecars. But nothing like being wrong on the internet helps standardize a term!

 At the end, I’m going to talk about two types of extension systems I’d like input on, one for sidecars, and one within records.

 Contents 

 Sidecar Pattern #1: Keys derived from the subject 

 Sidecar Pattern #2: Explicit reference in records 

 Sidecar Pattern #3: Record metadata object keyed by the collection’s NSID (proposed) 

 An alternative (#4): Namespaced, schema-defined extension fields embedded in the record 

 Open questions 

 Sidecar Pattern #1: Keys derived from the subject

 This covers:

 #A: Reusing the subject’s record key in another collection, e.g. app.bsky.feed.threadgate [ definition , example record ] ⇒ the Lexicon explicitly requires the threadgate to share the root post’s record key and repository

 #B: Deriving a key from the subject’s full AT URI, e.g. social.coves.community.acceptance [ definition , example record ] ⇒ the Lexicon specifies a an hash of the subject URI

 In this pattern, locating a sidecar from its subject depends on a convention. An app must already know which collection and repository to look in, and how to calculate the key.

 To help developers understand the relationship:

 Sidecar records may feature a link back to the subject

 The sidecar’s Lexicon description may document how to map sidecar ⇔ subject

 Strengths/weaknesses:

 Once the convention is known, an app can fetch a sidecar directly

 Metadata can be updated without giving write access to the subject record

 Metadata updates don’t create a new CID for the subject record

 Sidecars can support independently owned metadata by deriving keys from the full AtUri 

 Apps must know each sidecar’s collection, repository rules, and key derivation to look for it

 Changing the subject record’s key means migrating all sidecars or having an explicit policy for handling old associations

 Reusing only the subject’s record key may collide when different subject collections use the same key (e.g. self vs self on two separate Lexicons, avoided by #B )

 Sidecar Pattern #2: Explicit reference in records

 This covers:

 #A: From the sidecar to the subject, e.g. tech.transparencia.news.enrichment [ definition , example record ] ⇒ the Lexicon defines an article field referencing the subject’s URI and CID, alongside additional metadata

 #B: From the subject to the sidecar, e.g. place.atwork.endorsement [ definition , example subject , referenced proof ] ⇒ the Lexicon defines a signatures array containing AtUri + CID references to separate proof records attesting to the endorsement’s content

 In this pattern, the record stores an explicit reference, while the Lexicon defines what that reference means. This can also be combined with Pattern #1 , such as by reusing the subject’s key.

 To help developers understand the relationship:

 The reference points to the target’s repository, collection, and record key, which means:

 Subject ⇒ sidecar: an app can directly discover and fetch the referenced record.

 Sidecar ⇒ subject: finding sidecars that point to a record requires listing and filtering within repositories or maintaining an index

 The referencing field’s Lexicon description may document the semantics of the relationship

 Strengths/weaknesses:

 Differentiates subjects with the same key across both collections or repositories

 Subject ⇒ sidecar: an app reading the subject can locate the linked metadata directly

 Sidecar ⇒ subject: adding metadata does not require permission to edit the the subject (no CID change)

 Sidecar ⇒ subject: multiple apps can attach their own metadata

 Sidecar ⇒ subject: discovering sidecars requires a separate lookup mechanism (and potential enumeration, unless #1 is added)

 Subject ⇒ sidecar: attaching or changing the pointer requires write access to the subject and changes its CID 

 Moving or deleting the referenced record can leave dangling references

 A reference containing a CID identifies a specific version, which requires write permissions to the subject to update

 Sidecar Pattern #3: Record metadata object keyed by the collection’s NSID (proposed)

 I couldn’t find this pattern implemented, so this counts as a “proposal” of sorts. The most similar pattern I could find is:

 Metadata or configuration for a specific collection or XRPC method, e.g. at.inlay.endpoint [ definition , example record ] ⇒ the key is an XRPC method’s NSID, and its did field identifies the service implementing that method.

 …which can then be turned into a sidecar record keyed by collection with record key references inside the record.

 For example, in the example from the original forum post at://alice.example/community.lexicon.meta.links/app.bsky.feed.post could contain all the reverse links to app.bsky.feed.post s.

 {
 "$type": "community.lexicon.meta.links",
 "342hjkfsd": {
 "links": [
 {
 "href": "https://alice.example/posts/hello",
 "rel": "canonical"
 }
 ]
 },
 "342hjkxyz": {
 "links": [
 {
 "href": "https://alice.example/posts/another",
 "rel": "canonical"
 }
 ]
 }
}

 In this pattern, locating metadata depends on both the subject’s collection and its record key. An app fetches the sidecar record keyed by the collection’s NSID, then reads the entry matching the subject’s record key.

 For this example, the convention would be that the sidecar describes subjects in its own repository . So the 342hjkfsd entry refers to at://alice.example/app.bsky.feed.post/342hjkfsd . Metadata for place.stream.livestream/342hjkfsd would live in a separate sidecar record, keyed by place.stream.livestream .

 To help developers understand the relationship:

 The sidecar’s Lexicon description would document how the data is meant to be interpreted

 Each entry would have a defined metadata structure (see the links array above), although unions may be accepted

 Apps would still need to know which sidecar collections to query and their conventions. Known extension types can be fetched for with a single lookup.

 Strengths/weaknesses:

 When the convention is known, an app can locate metadata without an index or enumerating records

 Within a known sidecar collection, record keys immediately identify whether a subject collections has entries

 Can differentiate subjects with the same record key across collections (e.g. self records)

 Metadata updates do not modify the subject or change its CID 

 One fetch retrieves metadata for multiple subjects in the collection

 Current repository permissions cannot restrict an app to one target collection’s mapping

 The mapping grows with the number of subjects and can exceed record-size limits

 Updating one entry replaces the containing record and changes its CID 

 Concurrent writers updating different entries must coordinate to avoid overwriting each other’s changes

 Renaming or deleting a subject requires updating its entry

 An alternative ( #4 ): Namespaced, schema-defined extension fields embedded in the record

 The other approach I’d like input on is an alternative to sidecar records that puts additional information inside the subject record, in a field named after the Lexicon defining its contents .

 Both atmo.rsvp events and BridgyFed posts already add metadata inside records, so embedding extensions isn’t new. What I’m proposing is a shared way to name, document, and validate those extensions that avoids the risk of field-name collisions—one concern raised by [the spec’s recommendation]( https://atproto.com/specs/lexicon#authority-and-control ) against adding additional fields.

 This would be a shared convention:

 The field name is the extension Lexicon’s NSID (possibly with a prefix, here I used lex: )

 Its value conforms to the definition of that Lexicon

 The Lexicon documents what the extension means when attached to another record

 For example, a hypothetical extension to an app.bsky.feed.post could be:

 {
 "$type": "app.bsky.feed.post",
 "text": "Hello from my website!",
 "createdAt": "2026-10-18T12:00:00Z",
 "lex:community.lexicon.meta.links": {
 // this is optional, so we can't rely on it
 // without an associated special key, it also creates collision risks
 // "$type": "community.lexicon.meta.links",
 "links": [
 {
 "href": "https://alice.example/posts/hello",
 "rel": "canonical"
 }
 ]
 }
}

 Here, community.lexicon.meta.links (preceded by lex: ) would mean that the field is described by the Lexicon community.lexicon.meta.links . The post’s own $type remains app.bsky.feed.post .

 With this method, the extension travels with the record while telling developers where to find its definition. An app can notice that the additional data exists and identify its schema without already knowing which sidecar collection or repository to query.

 Strengths/weaknesses:

 An app (or app dev) reading the subject record can see that extension data exists

 Embedded metadata requires no additional record lookup

 The association is unambiguous, including across different collections

 Different record types can reuse the same extension definition

 Adding or updating metadata requires permission to edit the subject

 Validating the subject’s Lexicon does not automatically validate undeclared extensions

 Every metadata change changes the subject’s CID 

 Extensions increase the subject record’s size

 For larger or independently updated metadata, the extension could instead contain an AtUri pointing to a separate record.

 Open questions

 The obvious one: are there existing approaches I’ve missed, or tradeoffs I’m overlooking?

 For sidecars: is there interest in standardizing how to declare what they extend and how to locate the associated records?

 For embedded extensions: would this shared naming and validation convention be useful? Are there other patterns people would prefer?

 No pattern here fits every use case. Regardless, I’d still like apps to have a shared way to discover extensions and find their definitions without having to know about each one in advance, and without competing over the names and meanings of fields in someone else’s Lexicon.

This is a great overview.

 One thing that jumped out at me reading this was the idea of composition vs inheritance in system design.

 That got be thinking about mix-ins which is basically what adding fields to a record produces. I wonder if an extension to lexicons could be a way to declare additional types that the record should conform to? Something like a $types array with NSIDs. That would let you declare all the parts of the record shape that are joined together.

Wow, very comprehensive. Thank you @essentialrandom.bsky.social , this is great!

 First, and most important, I like your #4 proposal, especially if we strongly encourage people to also include $type , for clarity, even if it duplicates the field name itself.

 I’d be down to work on #4 with you, maybe starting with proxy links ( Connecting records, web pages and apps )?

 Beyond that, a few thoughts on on the other ideas. First, #1A is obviously my other preference here besides #4 , partly because Bluesky PBC themselves prefer it, but you’re absolutely right that the lack of discoverability hurts it.

 The hard thing we’re trying to do here is extend other people’s existing lexicons. I think that basically dismisses #2B , since that can only be done by a lexicon’s own authors.

 #2A has an extreme lack of discoverability that’s worse than any of the other options: afaict it requires a dedicated appview or similar index and lookup in order to find a given subject’s sidecars. (As opposed to eg #1A and #1B , which can be done with a single extra getRecord call to the PDS.)

 #1B seems…ok…but discoverability is worse than #1A , since the sidecar’s rkey is opaque.

 #3 I think is a non-starter due to the scaling limit and churn, which you mentioned.

It would be nice! But the history of extension systems for schema standards like this is…cautionary. XML, COM/CORBA, WSDL, schema.org , etc. The Bluesky team has been pretty clear that they’re not interested in trying it here, and I’m personally inclined to agree with them.

Thank you for making this.

 Personally I’m really interested in embedded extensions being solved, because I know examples of fields being added to records that lack any prefix, mainly via field added to posts by some Bluesky clients, so enforcing some conventions would be great. Makes me worried we could maybe have a similar situation to this: Lexicons, Pinned Posts, and Interoperability - AT Protocol . Also having extensions be tied to a lexicon is great and love that most people proposing solutions think the same.

 One thing I’m unsure about is if having them at the top-level is a good idea or not and if not would it being under some reserved/special field be better like $ext or similar. One benefit I can think of is it being easier to get all extensions without additional filtering.

value.title: Account Recovery with Rotation Keys
value.textContent:
I’ve been working on password reset and account recovery in atproto-pds and atproto-entryway, and I’ve landed on a feature I want to discuss broadly, get feedback on, and propose to the community.

 Problem

 Password and account recovery is strongly tied to email, and there aren’t any on-protocol or protocol-adjacent solutions that don’t require the identity to have immediate access to a single inbox. I have some mixed feelings about using email addresses and cell phone numbers that I’m not going to get into here, but the tl;dr is that reliance on them during an incident is precarious.

 There are lots of reasons that you may not have access to incoming email from your PDS operator including, and not limited to, not having access to a shared inbox and related shared-account woes, being locked out of an email account, DNS*, etc.

 Regardless, you’re left asking the operator for help, and on a network where the whole point is that your identity doesn’t depend on the operator’s goodwill, that’s a bad place to end up.

 Another thing that bugs me is that account holders already have a credential that outranks their account password: rotation keys. A rotation key on a did:plc identity can sign a PLC operation that moves the identity to a different PDS, and that is a much more powerful proof of ownership than a password. Letting a rotation key get you back into your account recognizes that holder’s authority.

 Design

 The existing password reset flow is established as a “request a token, use the token” process that incorporates email.

 To reset a password, the account holder needs to have both a server-generated token (like “ABCD-1234”) that was given to them by invoking the com.atproto.server.requestPasswordReset XRPC method with the email address associated with the account in question. The account holder then invokes the com.atproto.server.resetPassword XRPC method with both the token and password fields to change the account password.

 I propose minting and submitting an account recovery JWT token instead of the server-generated token. This account recovery JWT (as {"typ": "recovery+jwt"} ) proves ownership of the rotation key because only the holder can sign the JWT with it. A single-use, short-lived recovery JWT can be used in place of the PDS-generated token with the resetPassword XRPC method. From there, resetPassword works exactly as it does today.

 This is an addition, not a replacement. The account portal’s “enter your code and a new password” page is the same page for both paths. A client with an “I already have a code” screen works without knowing recovery keys exist.

 Solution

 The account recovery JWT is a compact JWS that describes the identity and signature proof, and includes reasonable, paved-path security constraints.

 The header includes the algorithm ( alg ), type ( typ ), and key identifier ( kid ). The JWT type limits this JWT’s use, so it can’t be confused with other token types, such as general OAuth access tokens or inter-service authentication tokens. The key identifier is the did-method-key serialized public key that must be byte-for-byte identical to one of the rotation keys ( rotationKeys ) in the DID document.

 The claims include the issuer ( iss ), audience ( aud ), issued at ( iat ), expiration time ( exp ), and JWT ID ( jti ). Both the issuer and audience are DIDs that map to the identity that issued the JWT and the identity meant to receive and process the token, in this case the PDS on which the identity’s account is on. The issued at and expires at claims ensure short-lived tokens are created to prevent possible abuse. The JWT ID ensures the token cannot be replayed, and servers that consume this type of account recovery token must take special care to prevent reuse.

 {
 "alg": "ES256K",
 "typ": "recovery+jwt",
 "kid": "did:key:zQ3sh…"
}
{
 "iss": "did:plc:ewvi7nxzyoun6zhxrhs64oiz",
 "aud": "did:web:mayon.pyroclastic.cloud",
 "iat": 1760000000,
 "exp": 1760000300,
 "jti": "Nk3n0WsT1F9m8Q2aXv7cLg"
}

 The typ does not reuse the existing jwt , at+jwt , or refresh+jwt consumed by the PDS. There is also no lxm because the type already scopes the token to a single, specific purpose.

 Rotation Key Constraints

 PLC lists rotation keys in order of authority. A key earlier in the list can override (within the 72-hour recovery window) an operation signed by a key later in it. A PDS holds rotation keys for its accounts so it can sign PLC operations on their behalf. The rule I landed on is that the key signing a recovery token must rank above every rotation key the service signs with.

 For example, if the rotation key list looks like [A, B, C, D] where the operator issues B and C , then only A could be used to recover an account.

 A key ranked below the service’s is a key the service can override, so it represents control the service could take back. A key ranked above can override the service. Only the second kind is the right thing to hang a reset credential on.

 There’s also a specific attack this closes. Someone who briefly holds a session and an email token can have the service sign a PLC operation that appends a rotation key. If any rotation key could mint a reset code, that appended key is a backdoor that survives a password change and an email change. Under this rule, it mints nothing, and the real holder, with a higher key, can remove it.

 Additionally, the service’s own keys never qualify. The operator can’t walk this path on its own accounts, and a leaked operator rotation key is not a reset credential for every account the service hosts.

 The set the rule compares against is the keys the service signs PLC operations with online. If a service has no rotation key for an identity at all, like an account that migrated while keeping its own keys, any rotation key qualifies. Granted, this is a weird edge case that I hope is just theoretical.

 Reference Implementation

 This is implemented and deployed as a feature of atproto-pds and atproto-entryway within atproto-crates. The atproto-identity crate has both recovery_token::mint and recovery_token::verify for minting and verifying the account recovery JWTs. The verifier takes the token, the accepted audiences, the current time, the lifetime ceiling, the identity’s current rotationKeys and the public halves of the service’s own keys. It hands back the verified claims or a typed refusal.

 atpdid recovery-token mints a token from a rotation key kept in a file or an environment variable. It reads the DID’s audit log, checks the key is a current rotation key, and prints the token on stdout. atpdid recovery-redeem takes that token and the new password and posts both to com.atproto.server.resetPassword . It sends them to the server the token is addressed to: the token’s did:web audience, or the PDS named in the issuer’s verified PLC log, unless --pds says otherwise. The two commands are separate so that the minting machine can stay offline.

 atpdid recovery-token --did did:plc:... \
 --aud did:web:mayon.pyroclastic.cloud \
 --key recovery.key > token.txt

atpdid recovery-redeem token.txt --password new-password.txt

 The resetPassword XRPC takes a token and a password, with both as plain strings. The server does a small shape-check to see if the token looks like a JWT, and then proceeds to parse it as an account recovery JWT if it does. This one call checks the token, spends it, and resets the password. The lexicon defines only InvalidToken and ExpiredToken , so any other refusal comes back as InvalidToken, with a message saying which check failed, which feels appropriately vague.

 The account portal’s forgot-password page offers two options: a code by email, or a recovery token plus a new password. atproto-entryway does the same for a cluster and accepts either its own DID or the hosting member’s DID as aud. A member PDS in entryway mode forwards resetPassword to the entryway, as it already did.

 Because it’s an existing method, there’s no lexicon to publish or resolve, and any client that can call resetPassword can redeem a recovery token. A server without the feature looks the token up as an emailed code, finds nothing, and answers InvalidToken. A server that has the feature but has it switched off says so in the InvalidToken message. It’s deployed on Mayon and Vesuvius, and you can see the whole flow at https://mayon.pyroclastic.cloud/account/password/forgot .

 Screenshot 2026-10-18 at 9.56.14 PM 2236×1612 252 KB 

 Closing

 I believe this is a worthwhile measure to ensure account holders can recover their accounts when they otherwise couldn’t. This builds on the strengths of did-method-plc and verification methods, and has the big benefit of not requiring any additional change to the existing password reset lexicon schema. The rank rule matches the authority model PLC already has instead of inventing one, and the verifier is a simple process that any implementation can lift.

 Counterarguments and caveats: it serves did:plc identities, and only those whose holder has set up a rotation key above the service’s, which today is a minority of accounts. It adds a token type every bearer-token verifier has to refuse. It puts PLC resolution behind an unauthenticated endpoint, which means rate limiting and caching are part of the implementation rather than nice-to-haves.

 The code is in the atproto-crates workspace: the token module is at https://tangled.org/ngerakines.me/atproto-crates/blob/main/crates/atproto-identity/src/recovery_token.rs .

I think this is pretty interesting and would align account management more directly with theory. That is, we talk about DIDs being the root of account identity in theory, and this would make that a bit more real.

 If you control an identity DID, it is already possible to do adversarial account migration, so in some sense this doesn’t feel like it would change the overall control and account security picture too much. did:web is an interesting case to consider because control can pass on to another party if the domain registration lapses (or I guess if it is hijacked).

 A thread modeling question is whether there is data which you can only get with account credentials on a specific host, and not with account identity control. The registered account email address is one example (assuming the PDS requires an email address). Things like chat.bsky.* DMs are accessed over XRPC, and an identity controller can mint service auth tokens. Space data which isn’t public could usually be accessed using identity control by requesting a space credential, then using that for requests to the account host.

 I think I am onboard with the overall direction of this. But i’m curious to hear what others thing.

 In terms of the details and prioritizing/sequencing this as an interoperable standard, I think it might take some time, at least for implementation in the Bluesky-maintained PDS distribution. There are some related open questions that might bundle up with this one: how does a PDS become aware of identity updates (PLC, did:web, or handle invalidation) for hosted accounts? How should the PDS treat accounts when the account identity is pointed to a different PDS instance? Should the PDS support hosting accounts with did:plc when the PDS has the atproto signing key, but doesn’t control any rotation keys (similar to how did:web works)?

Some follow-up thoughts:

 this feels a lot like passkeys. for everyday use and external ecosystem support, passkeys would probably go a long way, even if they don’t necessarily touch on the atproto identity concept

 currently PLC rotation keys are only used to sign PLC operations. could they even be used to sign JWTs if they were in a hardware enclave or something like that?

 an emergency recovery flow that would align more directly with how adversarial account migration works would be to have the account update their PLC identity with a new #atproto signing keypair that they control, and then use that to do an XRPC service auth request to the PDS to update the password

If the only PLC rotation keys are the ones held by the account host provider, this might complicate things here because of whoever holds the keys hold the accounts (aka the “Not your (rotation) keys, not your crypto Atmosphere account” part of non-custodian account management). While the host operators can require additional proof of identity in case of issues with their email address or 2FA, I would want to worry if an attacker (human or otherwise AI agent) deliberately accessed the secret keys and do nasty things there. That’s my two cents for now.

I like this direction very much, but would like to take it a step further and also allow it to do OAuth login’s and session creations directly ( you could do it anyway after a password reset )

 Actually it is more or less the same flow I used in my FedCM demo here:

 Bluesky Social – 19 Jan 26 

 Willem Dantuma (@willem.dobs.nl) 

 Here a demonstration how an ATProto login could look like with FedCM support, left /accounts of the PDS, middle the ATProto Oauth demo client (go) and right pdsls showing the result. The PDS FedCM /assertion endpoint creates a short lived idToken...

 and tried to discuss here:

 Bluesky Social – 17 Jan 26 

 Willem Dantuma (@willem.dobs.nl) 

 what we could do is let the FedCM /assertion endpoint return an id_token and use this as an id_token_hint in the PAR request and then continue the normal flow. We still need to go through the consent screen of the PDS @thisismissem.social how this...

 In this demo I used an id-token signed by the OAuth issuer as an id_token_hint in the OAuth flow but my preferred way would be to use a jwt token (deliberately not naming it id-token here to remove the OAuth relation ) proofing you possess a non operator owned (top level) rotation key.

 Also i would like to suggest to add client binding ( HTTP message signatures )

 It boils down to be able to identify yourself (login) with a jwt proofing you possess a top level rotation key instead of a password.

value.title: [Discussion/Ideas] The state of burnout and bus factors in the open social web
value.textContent:
Hello, fellow builders and open-sourcerers in the Open Social Web! I would like to chime in here in the Atmosphere Community forums (might cross-post to SocialHub in the Fediverse community) regarding what’s the current state of bus factors and people “getting hit by a bus”, especially in the gen AI era where (mostly unreviewed) AI-generated contributions and witch hunting from anti-AI purists (aka “pipebombing in the replies/DMs” in my own words) often cause developers to either slow down development or leave the community entirely. I want both honest and civil discussions of this sensitive topic without the parts that often burns everyone off the discourse.

 How did we got here?

 Let’s say it started with me asking Claude ( link to original transcript in case anyone asking) months ago about if there’s pre-existing academic/scientific literature regarding the bus factor situation that esclated quickly into planning to contribute into the open-source sustainability discourse by surveying the current state of these within the aforementioned ecosystems. Another reason why I this exist is that there were history of in-fighting between protocol devs and even its users alongside mass exodus of devs and users for different reasons from moderation and community toxicity ( see part one of Blacksky origin story series ) up to the “paid audits a la Matrix”-related headaches (as Soatok mentioned in his blog ).

 I’ll be also upfront about why I’m the one asking this here: I have an very autistic special interest in community health and how trust structures fail, and my pattern recognition is struggling not catch them up across every domain it pops out. The bus-factor conversation in OSS sustainability circles is really a smaller version of a much older pattern throughout the history — small groups holding a lot of keys to the kingdom (it’s a CGP Grey reference if you insist, but I am mentioning The Dictator’s Handbook and selectorate theory here for futher readings since it explains the mechanism part and not because I think it just excuses anyone), and what happens when that concentration breaks down, whether through burnout, departure, or in-fighting. I’ve watched variations of this happen in places well outside tech, including in my country’s political history, and the mechanics rhyme more than people usually expect. So this thread isn’t really is the bus factor bad but closer to what does it look like when a young, still-forming protocol ecosystem hits this failure mode before it's built the immune system older communities eventually grow .

 Agenda / Purpose

 The agenda / purpose of this thread is to:

 discuss about the bus factor/burnout situation among builders and open-source devs of both ecosystems in the public and share field notes about it

 develop a (informal) community survery regarding this either in the form(s) of asynchronous survey forms, usage of augur toolkit from CHAOSS project + TruckFactor and anecdotal notes from fellow developers and publishing its results (this could be optional, but I do not intend to turn this research into a capstone project at later years in college for reasons)

 Other ideas, anyone? Feel free to chime in as long as you follow the community guidelines here.

 Although honestly, I will be simply documenting things at the moment (maybe over at my digital garden) based on my current capacity as I am focused on academics lately as a college student but I’ll be open for collaborative work if you do.
It’s a bit late on my watch (0:31 Philippine Standard Time), but will be back after class hours (7:00-15:00) to reply around.

Fully accept I may be naive here but what is the topic, plainly? Are we talking about whether the ATP will die if the people who have access to Bluesky money decide to go elsewhere, or some different concern?

seantiz.com: 

 Fully accept I may be naive here but what is the topic, plainly? Are we talking about whether the ATP will die if the people who have access to Bluesky money decide to go elsewhere, or some different concern?

 It’s not just from the funding/sustainability part of the entire “bus factor” problem here but I also want to look at the community health parts of it, especially the internet toxicity problem that often plagued communities badly.

I would strongly recommend instead of trying to look at “why development communities fail” for you to look at wider trends in community building on class/race/gender lines and then comprehensively piece those overlapping patterns together, as well as a cross-analysis of the economic factors at play when trying to address this question.

value.title: Where do you get your news about the Atmosphere?
value.textContent:
I used to follow Laurens Hof’s ATmosphere report religiously. I loved that it included a broad spectrum of topics like significant app releases, protocol work, institutional developments, community movements and government involvement. But it seems he has moved on to other things and I haven’t been able to find good sources for general information about happenings in the atmosphere. I get a lot from this forum as well as various people’s blue sky accounts/blogs, but I can tell there’s a lot I’m missing. I would love to see where folks get their up-to-date ATmoNews.

 PS not sure if this should be in resources and learning, or just general discussion.

Thanks Sophie. This is you , right?

 @laurenshof.online still around @laurenshof.online on Bluesky 

 It’s probably a very good time to address this. Its almost impossible to get orientated around what started as a protocol’s development, and now, because that is changing so many aspects of “social” media, (networks, apps, etc) its near impossible to get a complete overview of quite revolutionary changes.

 A couple of views from my perspective.

 The governance of PDS operators as things move out of the original (USA) tech focus. (I’ll leave it for someone else to outline the latest view of large, and small, PDS operators.

 My approach, in any web community, is to follow the conferences. Next year’s Atmosphere conf is just starting to form up , so lots of different new (european) stuff will jump out of that, so you can track the movers and shakers.

 Lastly, and this isn’t a suck up. @bmann.ca is THE community man around this discourse tool & other AT traps. I keep trying to find a place where the AT community managers structure their “org chart”; something every newbie needs to get orientated. Well see. (really nice people though)

There is too much to follow! I generally look to boost things with the @atmosphere.community account.

 One of the ideas with the atmosphere.community website is that news can get aggregated there. It’s going to need some folks doing active curation at some point.

 It’s in flux and should probably have a big “under construction” banner as it moves to supporting spaces and groups.

 We got as far as trying to ingest things like an “atproto” or “atmosphere” tag and grouping those automatically. And/or using Skyreader / Standard Reader tools to expose such a grouping.

 So yeah, I’ve mostly mentioned some tooling, with perhaps the AC site being a spot where people volunteer to do more with it.

Semble Collections, following key people on Bluesky, this site and finding / following key blogs are really the best options right now IMO.

 I created a list of “ATproto tinkerers” which I use like a feed sometimes for the people I don’t want to follow and have in my main feed. There are a few other people who have built atproto feeds as well but I haven’t found them as useful as just following key people.

 Blog posts from people using Standard Site blogs is another discovery option at the moment: https://standard-reader.app/ Patrick Singletary and a few other people occasionally do summary blog posts like this where it doesn’t go in depth https://insummary.offprint.app/ and various people write in depth about the things that they are doing / interest them.

There were a couple experiments with automated digests but it’s hard to get the quality reliably good enough:

 Needed: Weekly Update Agent Discussion 

 Last year I could skim through the entire atproto feed(s) every day with relative ease. This year, to my great delight, that has become a challenge because there’s just so much going on. 
I still get primarily atproto stuff in my For You and I continue to occasionally check in on the atproto firehose so I can engage in real-time with at least my local section of The Latest. 
But to maintain my overview of the Atmosphere at large, I need a slower feed. Many tech communities have this sort of thin…

Hi! I’ve been curating a collection up-to-date and wide ranging news and discussion about the Atmosphere on Semble for the last year. It’s an open collection too, so other are more than welcome to help out and we’ve had a bunch of contributors in the past. While I used to also curate weekly summaries about this, it ended up taking too much time to do on my own, but it should be straight forward to create your own custom views/summaries over the collection.

 @bmann.ca maybe this collection could power news on atmosphere.community?

 semble.so 

 at://news (by 𝕮) — Semble 

 Collectively-curated weather reports of the atmosphere.

Hey Chris! Mostly “someone” will have to form a group and decide how to implement it.

 Ms Boba has a bunch of plans around Spaces and Groups which gives building blocks.

 Curating community news is going to be a big job. I hope some folks step up and take it on. There’s probably related work on how to share community assets like our large mailing list.

 Monthly summaries of just the bigger stuff could be a more sustainable option and might be sufficient for most folks. This could also be rotated.

I’d like to help build a developer outreach group for atproto. Folks who deliver high quality open source contributions to projects that would genuinely benefit from Atmospheric social features, atproto interoperability (or even just “Log in with Atmosphere†”).

 I’d propose that the members of ATproto Maker Outreach (eh?! ) would:

 Seek, accept suggestions for & track open source projects which might benefit from atproto integration

 Assess the right work to offer each project as a group, and how best to offer it

 Find & coordinate volunteers to complete the work. We’d:

 Keep the work small, self-contained and easy to review

 Collaborate internally to review the work before submitting it to the owners (this would be a great place for atproto learners!)

 Hold ourselves to the Human Responsible AI contribution policy (but hand-write, or move on, if the maintainers in question would prefer that)

 Offer our collective expertise on going deeper into atproto land, if the maintainers want it

 Contribute to (build?) the atproto community’s ‘best practices’ guides, and champion them

 Be kind, respectful and human at all points; make friends & have fun

value.title: Proposal: a community lexicon for standalone images
value.textContent:
The need

 I made this image . It is mine, and I am on the Atmosphere — I should be able to deploy it in N places as I go.

 The live case: I run EPTSS , a song-cover community that submits tracks through plyr.fm , and I build Luminframe , an atproto image editor. My users make art in Luminframe and publish music on plyr — their art should just be there as track artwork. I PR’d plyr to make that real, and plyr had to hard-code com.luminframe.image . Every reader learning every writer by name doesn’t scale; one shared collection does — n writers, readers wire up once. What standard.site did for long-form.

 Smaller than standard.site

 standard.site standardizes distribution — publications, subscriptions, a text fallback over many content formats. Images need less: the blob is the universal format — content, wrapper, and fallback at once. This is just the artifact layer that distribution can later point at.

 Prior art

 com.luminframe.image and social.grain.photo already write nearly this record independently. app.bsky.embed.images is embed-only. lexicon.community has no media namespace yet.

 Draft schema

 Provisionally community.lexicon.media.image — the name is yours, the shape is what I’ll defend. Full JSON attached.

 field 
 req 
 why 

 image (blob) 
 yes 
 the thing itself — content and fallback 

 aspectRatio 
 yes 
 layout before bytes arrive 

 createdAt 
 yes 
 natural ordering 

 alt 
 no* 
 the image’s voice when eyes can’t see it 

 *optional in schema, expected in practice.

 Absent by design: titles, galleries, EXIF, location. A field gets in when two independent implementers need it.

 Extensions and adoption

 Records are open — Luminframe’s standard records also carry its edit recipe ; generic readers ignore it. One record, one center. And since a blob can back multiple records in one repo, dual-publishing alongside your existing lexicon is zero extra storage and about an afternoon. Plyr’s whole migration is widening one constant.

 The ask

 If you write standalone image records — Grain especially — say where this doesn’t fit your schema. The goal: the next reader wires up once and gets everyone.

Instead of defining community.lexicon.media.* , I’d highly recommend making use of ing.dasl.masl , which is about resources in general:

 DASL 

 DASL: MASL — Metadata for Arbitrary Structures & Links 

 MASL is a CBOR-based metadata system that is designed to work well with content-addressed and decentralised systems, to enable fully self-contained, self-certified content distribution.

Hey @natespilman.at thanks for the write up. I do wish you had a handwritten introduction even if you got agent help in making the lexicon.

 I think this is interesting!

 The only other thing I can think of is a pattern that isn’t widely used yet - a raw/original/source field that points to an off protocol larger file.

 Or the reverse - as blobs get bigger, does it make sense to generate thumbnails and store them as blobs?

 Not my lexicon so up to you all to figure it out!

 You’re going to want to find at least one other person to co-lead with you.

Thanks Boris!!

 and sorry for the full AI output. I basically wrote 100% of my thoughts into the robot and refined it until I liked it, but I should have just done that on the page itself.

 thank you for your reply, and I’ll get back to y’all in a hand written manner soon!

How does one go about putting a lexicon in with ing.dasl.masl ? Is there a submission process to get one included under their top level?

 Or, is it that you’d make a new lexicon somewhere else (e.g. com.al9000.image ) and reference ing.dasl.masl somehow?

 Or, would this be something that could be submitted to community.lexicon.media but have the format from ing.dasl.masl ?

 (I’m new to this and haven’t figured out how that part works)

I really like MASL (and tiles), but I do want to point out that the lexicon schema for ing.dasl.masl as it is currently deployed ing.dasl.masl Documentation (EN) - Lexicon Garden doesn’t look like that.

Lexicon Community lives here, the blog is our announce / info / source of truth info.

 And yes, this lexicon from you is big and opinionated.

 We’re encouraging people to scope things down as @natespilman.at has – what is the minimum viable useful for everyone starting point – this gives applications a way to add records in different ways while having the broadest amount of compatibility to aggregate “all images”.

 This would be the work of a working group to come to consensus, but here are some blink reactions from me:

 copyright is immediately going to be contentious and of course applies to things that aren’t images

 two sets of tags in one record smells bad - why wouldn’t this be an individual image and then point to this as various sorts of collections (e.g. a Grain album)?

 (no need to respond or argue this, this is just offered as an example rabbithole which is not strongly held by me)

 And, rather than jumping into “here’s what the fields would be”, I would recruit 2+ implementors or intent-to-implementors so this is informed by people that will actually be deploying this.

 Nate gave us a thumbnail sketch of something to get started, which is great – now socialize what apps would implement this, THEN form the working group.

Oh I have just started thinking about something similar

 cultureblocs.com 

 com.cultureblocs.creative.work - Protocol — CultureBlocs 

 Nine small ATProto lexicons under the com.cultureblocs.* namespace — anchored to this domain, which is what makes them citable. The same shapes describe a record on a device, in a self-hosted spine, or published to the open network; privacy is a...

 I’ve been thinking about a set of small data pieces partially around personal note taking on cultural activity (read this book, went to this gallery, etc) but also a lightweight creator note (I made this etc) just enough to have its existence as a hook available , so others could link it with ( I read this book - link to book culturebloc)

 Similarly for venues and shows , I’ve already switched to the lexicon community rsvp etc

 interested in being a part of this discussion.

 Mark

Interested in this. I’m going to do what I did for the app community lexicon: look at how existing lexicons use/store images and identify commonalities + divergences. That should narrow what this looks like, though I think the initial proposal and the one suggested that’s MASL-ish are good starts.
oh and @al9000.com I agree that pixel width and height make more sense than aspect ratio. aspect ratio can be derived from width and height, but not the other way around.
and @Marksimpkins - I really like the CultureBlocs idea. Would love the collab.

I’m totally on board with a smaller, more focused target lexicon. One of my aspirational project is a website builder/CMS that rides on AT Proto. My thinking was from that perspective. Moving forward on something with better general usage makes complete sense.

Yeah in my head I see this as just giving every blob a record (in this case, an image blob). I suspect a general blob record would need too much to make it useable? But worth considering if that’s not the case (thinking scope here; if record for a blob isn’t generalizable enough then the scope gets too big and just image blobs makes sense).
I think there could be something interesting here for “file” metadata if someone wanted to make general file storage out of blobs. But files aren’t images - so yes keep the scope smaller.

I like the idea, as @byarielm.fyi suggested, we can implement this generic file ownership pattern, beginning with file.type === image . Though I think this would require even more community buy in for how low level it is.

Yup after looking at lexicons I would agree. It’s likely more valuable to have an image-specific lexicon, video-specific, etc - more scoped to file types type lexicons.

 Here’s the table of lexicons - lexicons with images - fyi - pckt 

Not exhaustive because there’s so many lexicons now, but think this is pretty representative of how images are used and represented in records + I included some to demonstrate how this can be used widely as a catch-all.
cool, yeah happy to collab

This lexicon proposal looks good to me, and I agree with the use of dimensions instead of aspect ratio.

 Next steps - reach out to the publishers of the lexicons that @byarielm.fyi assembled and ask prettyplease to crosspost to this new lexicon?

 What’s the governance around the creation of the community.lexicon.media.image lexicon in the first place?

 Thanks!

From what I saw in reviewing, your ‘dimensions’ is what ‘aspectRatio’ actually is under all the lexicons. Some have it defined in the same lexicon, others have it in another.

 Probably easier to get but in if we use the same language even if it’s confusing lol

Also, regarding additional information like copyright, this is a great use case for a sidecar lexicon. For example, platform-specific metadata may be done as (pseudo-coded):

 Image record:

 key: cool-image
$type: community.lexicon.media.image
data: 
 - the blob
 - the alt text
 - the aspect ratio

 and then in the same PDS, the application-specific data can be:

 key: cool-image
$type: cool.application.image.metadata
data: 
 - filters used
 - version of software
 - title/description

 we could consider using this pattern for licensing information too, but we should first focus on getting the image lexicon itself adopted by the ecosystem.

essentialrandom.bsky.social: 

 One “concern” about precise dimensions: can the PDS ever (for example) resize the image in the blob to save space? In that case, dimensions may end up out of sync, while aspect ratio will be always be accurate.

 If a PDS (or any other process) changes the size of the image it should update the pixel dimensions as well. I don’t know if there’s a MUST way to require that, but if the listed pixel dimensions don’t match those of the blob, the record is effectively invalid. Any app relying on the pixel info will be working off faulty data.

 essentialrandom.bsky.social: 

 width / height descriptions should accurately describe what assumptions user should make. For example, if resizing is possible, then “the maximum height” and/or “the height of the image when saved”.

 In the same vein, if a process changes the image size without updating the pixel dimensions the user can no longer safely use the values to make assumptions. (I might be missing something with the max height, but if an image is uploaded with a given height, but a process changes the blob, the value can no longer be trusted regardless.)

 essentialrandom.bsky.social: 

 And, regarding pixel size: how does that work with SVGs or other vector-based image formats?

 Ah, right. I was implicitly thinking about this as only raster based images. My instinct is to make that explicit and create a second lexicon for vector based art. There’s enough difference between the two of them that it feels weird to have them in the same spot. If they end up in the same lexicon the usage requirements go up non-trivially for end users in terms of having to handle both types (e.g. if I’m using it for an avatar on a website, the code I generate for the output has to change between raster/vector).

Regarding size changes etc, some snippets from Blobs - AT Protocol :

 It is effectively not supported to dynamically serve assets directly out of blob storage (the getBlob endpoint) directly to browsers and web applications. Applications must proxy blobs, files, and assets through an independent CDN, proxy, or other web service before serving to browsers and web agents, and such services are expected to implement security precautions.

 and

 Servers are strongly recommended against parsing media files (image, video, audio, or any other non-trivial formats) directly, without the use of strong sandboxing mechanisms. In particular, PDS instances themselves should not directly implement media resizing or transcoding.

 Also, I believe changing dimensions would also change the CID and therefore the blob link.

I just made a post in the book lexicon thread about pondering if it makes sense to think about them like video file containers and payloads. The same question applies here. Instead of copy/pasting it (and having to change all the examples from books to images), I’m just gonna link it if you want to take a look:

 In Which A Book Lexicon is Born WG Books 

 This literally came to me in a dream: Does it make sense to think of book lexicons like video file formats? 
For example, the .mkv format is “a container format that can hold an unlimited number of video, audio, picture, or subtitle tracks in one file.” The stuff can be of different types (e.g. encoded with different video and audio codecs). 
In a similar manner, would it make sense to have a top level lexicon that functions as a container that you put other stuff in? Like a minimal root level l…

Hello folks!

At the last lexicon.community meeting I was (very gladly!) voluntold to help bring this lexicon to the finish line as the TSC representative.

 We’ve had a lot of discussions here about possible bells and whistles to add! I know there’s a lot of interest for things like credits, copyright, tags, etc. (not to mention even more things to build on top, like galleries, comics, etc.).

 That said, it’s generally best to have a simple base lexicon that can be used and reused in a lot of different applications, and then define “hook points” for further expansion. There also seems to be general consensus here over the base definition (multi-language alt text, dimensions, creation metadata, etc.).

 Given this, here’s how I’m thinking of moving this forward:

 I’m going to open a PR with the simple definition we converged towards so we have a solid initial base to start from

 Once it’s open, I’ll post it here, open it up for comments, and publish it more widely to get everyone’s wisdom in

 Separately, given the interest, we can start thinking about other extensions we may want to push forward, and apps that may want to work with us to standardize some of what we’ll be doing. If there’s enough interest, that could turn into its own WG.

 @byarelm.fyi did a lot of great research on how image Lexicons are currently being used, so that seems a great starting point to let what’s out there lead development rather than building a priori

 Do let me know if you want to be involved and have thoughts

Happy to help 

 Also want to note that I think atproto self labels should be part of the base lexicon here; we should encourage self labeling.

value.title: Is/not micro-reviews for Atmsopheric apps!
value.textContent:
https://isnot.at is a lexicon & demonstration site for a proposal I made a while ago for micro-reviews.

 It lets you review any subject represented by an at-uri with any number of ( direction + adjective ) tags, eg. “ The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy is really funny ”, or “ Puzzmo is cool ”.

 I thought it might be a good way for Atmospheric apps to model tagging/thumbs/stars/reviews so they can work across apps, and allow both simplicity and nuance where it’s needed.

 The next things I’d build would be data-science based; xRPC endpoints that recommend adjectives which would help you explore your opinions on a thing (Marmite: is/not delicious ?) and, if this takes off, recommendation algorithms based on the aggregate dataset. (it even support multiple locales, and could use k-means clustering to make the actual locale of a tag irrelevant, it’d just look at what tags you use for the things you like, and match that to the aggregate).

 The docs show how it works, with an interactive demo. Let me know what you think!

Greetings—the combination of a small shared model and room for nuance is interesting to us. PIXIE’s Atmosphere guide is intended to help people find a starting point, and we’re exploring how useful observations could travel between apps.

 How would you distinguish a personal impression from a dated accessibility observation—for example, “I tested this flow with VoiceOver on iPad”? Could supporting context accompany a review, or would you keep that in a separate record? We’d want to preserve someone’s experience without turning one successful test into a blanket accessibility claim.

I think I’d treat “an assessment” (an attempt at something objective) as distinct from “a review/ rating ” (something explicitly subjective), so I’d probably put accessibility observations like what you describe into a separate record type.

 I imagine you’d want to be able to index sites/apps on different aspects of accessibility (some folks value VoiceOver on iPad, some TalkBack on Android, etc) so I think you’d want to model your own dataset, so you could make the use-cases for the data more targeted than what I’ve put together here
