App Lexicon Working Group — Proposal Draft

 Status: DRAFT

 Authors: pixeline.be (Alexandre Plennevaux), byarielm.fyi (Ariel M. Lighty), jluther.net (John Luther)

 Date: 2026-04-25

 Part 1: Lexicon Design Proposal

 Context

 The AT Protocol ecosystem is growing fast. Multiple independent efforts currently track apps, tools, and services — from Semble collections (200+ apps) to BlueskyDirectory.com , atproto.brussels , AlternativeProto , sdk.blue , and more. At one point, there were 21 separate lists.

 There is no shared, machine-readable way to describe what an app is , what it does , or how it plugs into ATProto . This makes discovery fragmented and maintenance duplicative.

 Prior Art

 atproto.garden (dame.is): The most developed starting point. Defines garden.atproto.directory.submission — a record type stored on users’ PDS with fields like name, tagline, description, url, category, tags, projectState, creators, logo, screenshots, and lexicon metadata. Open source at github.com/dame-is/atproto-garden .

 store.stucco.software (nikolas.ws): Working implementation that creates records to PDS and checks rel=me for verification. Building an AppView that listens to the firehose.

 BlueskyDirectory.com ( jluther.net ): Largest meta-listing. Willing to participate.

 atproto.brussels (pixeline.be): Maintains a curated directory with fields like name, url, platform, short description, category, alternative_to, last_checked. Experiments with PDS-stored user ratings ( brussels.loves.appRating ).

 SoftwareApplication - Schema.org Type : Established web vocabulary for describing software applications.

 W3C Web Application Manifest / MASL : Manifest structures for web apps, noted as structurally similar by ngerakines.me and bmann.ca.

 ATProto OAuth client metadata : Already contains some app info (name, logo, urls) for apps that implement OAuth.

 Design Principles (distilled from the thread)

 Start minimal — resist scope creep (bmann.ca’s consistent message). Ship a small, useful set; iterate via PRs.

 Apps first — leave SDKs, infrastructure, and libraries for a future, separate lexicon.

 Resolve, don’t store — handles should be resolved from DIDs, not stored redundantly (byarielm.fyi).

 Signals over taxonomy — rather than a rigid category tree, expose small composable signals (type, capabilities, tags) that consumers can assemble into their own views (pixeline.be).

 self rkey convention — if the app’s official ATProto account publishes its own record with rkey self , that’s a self-attestation of ownership (zicklag.dev).

 Verification is out-of-band — verification (via rel=me , .well-known , or other methods) is a concern for directories/clients, not the lexicon itself. The lexicon just provides the data.

 App icon — apps upload their icon as .png or .jpeg to a designated space on the lexicon to make it easy to display the right app icon. I suggest 1000x1000 (bsky.app compresses to this (if not mistaken).

 "appIcon": { 

 "type": "blob", 

 "accept": ["image/png", "image/jpeg"], 

 "maxSize": 1000000 } 

(dave.self.surf)

 App svg — same as above, support .svg so others can display the logo on their app (eg., let me show my roomy icon in the footer).

(dave.self.surf)

 Proposed Lexicon: community.lexicon.app.entry 

 Below is a proposed minimal lexicon for describing an app in the ATProto ecosystem. It draws heavily from the atproto.garden schema, simplified per thread consensus.

 "lexicon": 1,
 "id": "community.lexicon.app.entry",
 "defs": {
 "main": {
 "type": "record",
 "description": "An app entry describing an app built on or for the AT Protocol. This record may be published by third parties or by the app itself. When an official self-published app profile exists, consumers should prefer that profile as the canonical record.",
 "key": "tid",
 "record": {
 "type": "object",
 "required": ["name", "url", "recordCreatedAt"],
 "properties": {
 "name": {
 "type": "string",
 "maxLength": 200,
 "maxGraphemes": 100,
 "description": "The display name of the app."
 },
 "url": {
 "type": "string",
 "format": "uri",
 "description": "The primary URL for the app, such as its website, landing page, or install page."
 },
 "description": {
 "type": "string",
 "maxLength": 1000,
 "maxGraphemes": 300,
 "description": "A short description of what the app does."
 },
 "logo": {
 "type": "blob",
 "accept": ["image/png", "image/jpeg", "image/webp", "image/svg+xml"],
 "maxSize": 500000,
 "description": "Primary logo for display. Should preferably be square."
 },
 "tags": {

 "maxLength": 10,

 },

 What’s intentionally left out (for now)

 These were discussed but deferred to keep v1 minimal:

 Screenshots, keyFeatures — useful for rich directories but not core metadata.

 customLexicons / supportedLexicons — valuable for developer-facing directories, but unlikely to be kept up-to-date by most submitters. Can be a v2 addition or a separate linked record.

 creators array — the submitter’s DID is already the record author. A brandDid covers the brand/org case. Full contributor lists can come later.

 alternative_to — interesting idea (raised by pixeline.be, supported by yamarten.bsky.social), but adds complexity. Better as a separate record type or tag convention.

 Verification — per thread consensus, verification is out-of-band. Directories can verify using self rkey convention, rel=me , .well-known , or their own criteria.

 Ratings / reviews — atproto.garden already has separate lexicons for these ( garden.atproto.directory.upvote , .review , etc.). These should remain separate from the directory entry itself.

 The self rkey convention

 When the app’s official ATProto account creates the record with rkey self (instead of a TID), it signals: “I am the official account for this app.” Any ATProto user can independently verify this by checking that the record’s author DID matches the brandDid (or is the only DID associated). This convention is borrowed from how app.bsky.actor.profile/self works.

 Third-party users can also submit entries about apps (using a normal TID rkey), which lets community members list apps whose developers haven’t created records themselves.

 Part 2: Working Group Template (filled out)

 Name

 App Directory Lexicon Working Group 

 Representatives

 Lexicon Community TSC: @bmann.ca 

 WG Lead: @pixeline.be (Alexandre Plennevaux)

 The Working Group lead is not expected to be the most experienced member on the topic of the WG, but is in charge of:

 Providing updates to the TSC representative about progress made

 Make sure that WG progress is happening regularly, or (if it’s not happening) that there is a defined plan for when work will restart

 Objective

 Define a minimal, community-maintained ATProto Lexicon for describing apps in the atmosphere, so that multiple directories, listings, and discovery tools can interoperate on a shared data format — stored in users’ PDS repos and available via the firehose.

 Aims & Deliverables

 [Last updated: 2026-03-20]

 Aim 1: Research and consolidate existing approaches 

 Survey the data models currently used by atproto.garden, BlueskyDirectory, atproto.brussels, store.stucco.software, AlternativeProto, Semble collections, and the ATProto OAuth client metadata spec. Identify the common core fields and the points of divergence.

 Deliverable: A comparison document mapping fields across existing directories

 Status: Partially done (the original thread has surfaced most of the data)

 Aim 2: Define a v1 App Directory Entry lexicon 

 Produce a minimal lexicon (record type) for an app directory entry, covering: identity (name, url), presentation (description, logo), classification (category, tags, platforms, project state), and provenance (brandDid, createdAt).

 Deliverable: A lexicon JSON file in the Lexicon Community repo, with accompanying documentation

 Status: In progress (proposal above)

 Aim 3: Document the self rkey convention and verification guidance 

 Write a short specification for how official app accounts signal ownership, and how directory consumers can verify entries using out-of-band methods (rel=me, .well-known, etc.).

 Deliverable: A guidance document in the Lexicon Community repo

 Status: Not started

 Aim 4: Build or adapt at least one working implementation 

 At least one app (AppView + client) should use the finalized lexicon to create records on PDS and display a directory. atproto.garden and store.stucco.software are both candidates.

 Deliverable: A working, open-source directory app that reads/writes the shared lexicon

 Status: In progress (nikolas.ws and dame.is are both building)

 Timeline

 [Last updated: 2026-03-20]

 Research & consolidation: 2 weeks (much already done in the thread)

 Lexicon v1 definition: 3-4 weeks from WG formation

 Verification guidance: Can run in parallel, ~2 weeks

 Working implementation: 4-6 weeks (can overlap with lexicon finalization)

 Current Members

 [Last updated: 2026-04-25]

 @pixeline.be (Alexandre Plennevaux) — maintains atproto.brussels , proposing to lead the WG

 @byarielm.fyi 

 Interested contributors from the original discussion thread : @dame.is @nikolas.ws @zicklag.dev @jluther.net @flo-bit.dev @yamarten.bsky.social 

 If you’d like to formally join the WG, you can edit the wiki to add your name to the bulleted list above and remove it from the ‘interested contributors’ line.

 Meeting Details and How to Join

 [Last updated: 2026-03-20]

 Where: TBD — likely a dedicated channel on the ATProto Community Discord, with async discussion on the Discourse forum

 When: Bi-weekly video/voice calls (day/time to be decided by members), with ongoing async work between meetings

 Who to contact: pixeline.be (on Discourse or Bluesky) if meetings haven’t happened in a while

 How to join: Post in the Discourse thread or reach out to any current member. New members should:

 Read this proposal and the original thread

 Be willing to contribute to lexicon design, implementation, or testing

 Ideally, be building or maintaining a directory/listing of ATProto apps

 What makes a good member: We’re looking for people who are actively maintaining app directories or building tools for ATProto app discovery. We especially need people who are ready to implement the lexicon in real apps — either by adapting existing directories or building new ones. Experience with ATProto lexicon design or app store / directory taxonomy is a plus, but enthusiasm and commitment to ship something minimal are more important.

 Stretch Goals and Long-term Explorations

 SDK / Library lexicon — a separate record type for developer resources (SDKs, libraries, infrastructure tools). Deliberately excluded from v1 to keep scope tight.

 Rich metadata extensions — screenshots, key features, supported/custom lexicons, OAuth client ID linking. These can be added as optional fields or separate linked records once v1 is stable.

 alternative_to relationships — a way for apps to declare what mainstream product they’re an alternative to (e.g., “alternative to Instagram”). Could be a separate record type that references directory entries.

 Cross-directory trust / curation signals — standardized way for directories to endorse or curate entries (the “trust signal” concept from zicklag.dev). Relates to labeling and moderation.

 Automated health checking — conventions for directories to report whether an app’s URL is still live.

 schema.org alignment — mapping the lexicon to SoftwareApplication - Schema.org Type for SEO and web interoperability.

 Curated lists — a meta-feature allowing anyone to create and publish a curated subset of directory entries (e.g., “Best photo apps”, “Tools for developers”).

 Additional Notes and References

Hey folks 

 We’re about a month into the spaces alpha! From what I can tell, it’s going along pretty nicely. We pushed out one breaking change about two weeks back, but it’s been pretty stable apart from that.

 I wanted to share a list of some of the open questions we’re still noodling on. Many of these will likely involve breaking changes. Most of these are not truly “open”, we have opinions on them and need to just nail it down. However, if anything is important to you, please share your thoughts.

 We’re hoping to hit all of these (and any other changes of similar scope) by end of October.

 Any change we make will first be made as a PR on the proposal repo . Then it will be merged when the implementation is updated and deployed. This happens on Thursdays and will be recorded in the alpha updates Discourse thread .

 If you missed it, we’ll be doing an office hours session on Thursday (sept 24) to chat about the alpha, answer questions, and collect feedback.

 Open write spaces

 Should the PDS offer spaces that anyone can write to?

 Proposal merged: 0016 Atproto spaces: simplespace write access by dholms · Pull Request #105 · bluesky-social/proposals · GitHub 

 Space credential expiration/revocation

 Do we need a revocation path?

 Should expiration be shorter than 2 hrs?

 Current proposal: 0016: Shorten expiration time and add revocation method by dholms · Pull Request #109 · bluesky-social/proposals · GitHub 

 Public spaces

 Are public spaces in any way different from permissioned spaces?

 Should space authorities be able to mint a credential when no delegation token is offered (ie unauthenticated)?

 Of course this is always “possible”, but is it considered “offspec”?

 Could/should public space repos be rebroadcastable (ie signed)?

 DID docs

 Do we definitely want new service/key identifiers?

 What exactly are the semantics?

 For instance, can space authority sign a space credential with their #atproto key (specified through kid claim) if they also have an #atproto_space key in their DID document?

 Repo serialization

 The currently-specced serialization format sucks.

 Should this be a CAR file? Or should it be a new format? (for instance STAR-lite )

 Do we need a “multi-repo” format used in account migration?

 DPoP

 Is this the right fit in the credential flow?

 Technically specified for OAuth.

 We could have our own construction using HTTP signatures or similar

 getSpaceCredential

 Can you use other types of proofs besides delegation token & client attestation?

 re: 0016 make getSpaceCredential more generic? · Issue #97 · bluesky-social/proposals · GitHub 

 Commits and signatures

 Should signatures be on the commit or should they be transferred as metadata (ie in HTTP headers)?

 Should we offer a deniable signature on single-record requests? (ie via com.atproto.space.getRecord )

 I think Bryan convinced me that the HMAC signing scheme needs a consumer-provided nonce. Expect some sort of tweak here

 Account status

 What is the account status of a space authority?

 Is it the same as normal account status? Can #atproto_pds and #atproto_space_host vary?

 Sync scaling/reliability

 Can we make write notifications less lossy?

 Does PDS (space repo) need to remember and retry notifications to space host?

 Does space host need to provide better self-healing mechanisms?

 Space deletion

 Is the deletion flow robust enough? It is lossy & best-effort.

 Do members need to receive a notification of space deletion? Or does just syncers suffice, and applications re in charge of informing members?

 URI scheme

 Should we try to resolve IETF syntax issue for space URIs (ie dropping slashes, ie just at: )

 Should we support either blobs or versioned records in space URIs (things we’ve wanted in public URIs but just haven’t gotten around to)?

Thank you for laying out the questions for the post-alpha phase. I look forward to Spaces becoming a foundation for a wide range of apps. I support a design that provides shared mechanisms for authorization and sync while leaving apps and Space authorities to decide the policies appropriate to their use cases.

 Below are my comments from an app implementation and operations perspective, including points I support, concrete use cases, and behavior I would like to clarify.

 Open write spaces

 I support open write spaces. They would be useful for receiving information, such as membership requests or inquiries, from people who have not already been registered as members. Independent read and write settings are particularly useful here: being able to submit something should not imply being able to read other people’s submissions.

 Space credential expiration/revocation

 I support shorter credential lifetimes combined with an explicit revocation mechanism. Using short lifetimes as the baseline, with revocation of individual credentials when access needs to be withdrawn sooner, seems like a good way to make revocation take effect promptly without requiring a call to the authority on every read.

 Public spaces

 For public spaces, I think the specification should allow a Space authority to issue read credentials without a delegation token. It seems natural that an app should not need to maintain someone’s user session just to retrieve public information. I support keeping the same data structures and sync APIs for public and private spaces while allowing the conditions for issuing credentials to differ.

 I also support signatures that remain verifiable after redistribution, so that data from public spaces can be authenticated when retrieved from mirrors or archives.

 DID docs

 I support dedicated service and key identifiers for Spaces. The option to continue using #atproto_pds and #atproto also seems useful for migration from existing services.

 Allowing Space Credentials to be signed with #atproto even when a dedicated key is present should be an option for compatibility, rather than a requirement for every Space authority.

 Repo serialization

 For serializing a single repo, I would prefer CAR if it meets the requirements, since it allows reuse of existing libraries and tools. I am also interested in formats such as STAR-lite, but I think the choice should be based on how much they improve transfer size, memory usage, and implementation complexity for the data structures used by Spaces.

 A format that bundles multiple repos would be useful for account migration and backups. Reusing the serialization format for individual repos within that bundle would make it easier to share implementation between routine sync and migration.

 DPoP

 I support continuing to use DPoP. When the same Space Credential is presented to multiple repo hosts, binding it to the presenter’s key seems appropriate to prevent a host that receives the credential from reusing it to access another host.

 There is also value in reusing implementations and experience from AT Protocol’s use of OAuth. As long as its application to Spaces can be clearly specified, I do not think the fact that DPoP was defined for OAuth is, by itself, a reason to choose a different mechanism.

 getSpaceCredential

 I support allowing getSpaceCredential to work with authorization methods that do not require a user’s delegation token. For example, a backup or search indexing service explicitly authorized by a Space administrator should not need to keep maintaining and refreshing a particular user’s OAuth session for ongoing sync.

 It would be useful to establish the service’s identity through client attestation and issue a Space Credential based on explicit permission granted to that service by the Space authority. This would allow access for services to be managed independently of individual user sessions, while repo hosts continue to use the same Space Credential verification mechanism.

 Commits and signatures

 I support providing deniable signatures for individual record fetches as well. For example, a client displaying just one linked post, or a tool fetching only the records it needs, would benefit from being able to verify those records without syncing the entire repo.

 For permissioned data, it would be good for these partial fetches to preserve deniability in the same way as regular repo sync.

 Account status

 If #atproto_pds and #atproto_space_host can be operated as separate services, I support treating their account statuses independently as well. For example, someone might deactivate their PDS account for public posts while continuing to act as the authority for a community Space hosted by a separate service.

 Deactivating an account on one service should not necessarily imply deactivating it on another service associated with the same DID. I think the design should distinguish the availability of an author’s records from their active status as a Space authority.

 Sync scaling/reliability

 It would be good to have a mechanism for retrying write notifications from repo hosts to Space hosts after an outage. I am particularly concerned about a new writer’s first notification being lost, with no subsequent writes. If the Space host does not know about that writer, wouldn’t the writer remain undiscoverable even if a syncer periodically checks listRepos ?

 I would like a guarantee that the writer can be discovered and synced in this case without requiring another write. If notifications can be coalesced to the latest revision of each repo, there should be no need to retain and resend every write notification individually.

 Space deletion

 I support sending Space deletion notifications to syncers and leaving member notifications to apps. How users should be notified depends on the use case, and I do not think the Spaces protocol needs to require enumerating all readers or managing their notification destinations for this purpose.

 I also support using SpaceDeleted during credential renewal to detect deletion when a notification has been missed. Distinguishing deletion from a temporary failure would let syncers proceed with deleting their local copies and derived data without depending solely on receiving a notification.

 URI scheme

 I support adopting a format that conforms to standard URI syntax, provided that Spaces will not end up using a mixture of the existing AT URI format and the new URI format. I see value in integration with existing link handling, such as treating references in documents as links in native apps and opening them in an app that handles the scheme.

 I also support being able to reference a blob or a specific version of a record with a single URI. This would be useful for linking to attachments and making it explicit which version of a document or post is being cited.

dholms.xyz: 

 Sync scaling/reliability

 Can we make write notifications less lossy?

 Does PDS (space repo) need to remember and retry notifications to space host?

 Does space host need to provide better self-healing mechanisms?

 I was about to make a separate topic but noticed this was here and this is niche-ish sync concern.

 Just had a longer talk on the atproto touchers discord about recovering from situations where an appview looses it’s list of spaces it has access to for whatever reason. A bit upside of public atproto data is that, assuming your app is properly designed, you can more or less nuke your appview DB and fully or mostly fully recover your whole app just from backfill. Spaces are harder in this regard though since even the existence of a space is potentially permissioned knowledge. So if you end up “forgetting” you have access to a space you might never know when trying to backfill. For that use case it would probably be nice for space hosts to expose a “hey there space host do you have any spaces for me?” endpoint. An authenticated endpoint that services (or any identity really) can make calls to to get a list of all spaces that that space host is willing to offer that identity access to to some degree. Could be styled as a spaces version of listReposByCollection . This could feasibly also be part of space-management implementations instead of the core spaces protocol. But I think it’s worth having a generic option. Or at the very least not leaving simplespace out of it if we do decide this should be a space-management thing not a core protocol thing.

 Other stuff here I have an opinion on:

 dholms.xyz: 

 DID docs

 Do we definitely want new service/key identifiers?

 What exactly are the semantics?

 For instance, can space authority sign a space credential with their #atproto key (specified through kid claim) if they also have an #atproto_space key in their DID document?

 and

 dholms.xyz: 

 Account status

 What is the account status of a space authority?

 Is it the same as normal account status? Can #atproto_pds and #atproto_space_host vary?

 I think we definetly want space hosts to have dedicated service and key entries. I don’t have a strong opinion on the currently proposed fallback behaviour, though I might argue that not having a fallback is simpler conceptually. Similarly allowing use of an arbitrary key entry with the kid claim follows the now established pattern of how atproto JWTs work so I’d argue it’s good to keep that going. For ease of use, implementation and understanding by everyone.

 Most importantly I think that having a connected space host should not constitute that identity having an account. That resolves the account status question: space authorities have no account status unless they also have an account at a PDS, and if they do then it follows the same semantics as for all other identities with accounts. Space authorities are a lot more similar to service identities than user identities and we should treat them more as such in my opinion.

 dholms.xyz: 

 Commits and signatures

 Should signatures be on the commit or should they be transferred as metadata (ie in HTTP headers)?

 Should we offer a deniable signature on single-record requests? (ie via com.atproto.space.getRecord )

 I think Bryan convinced me that the HMAC signing scheme needs a consumer-provided nonce. Expect some sort of tweak here

 I think signature should be in the commit. Mainly makes the commit object self contained but also makes it better suited for potential future transports (or apps choosing specific custom transports).

 Single-record deniable signature would be really good if you ask me.

 dholms.xyz: 

 Public spaces

 Are public spaces in any way different from permissioned spaces?

 Should space authorities be able to mint a credential when no delegation token is offered (ie unauthenticated)?

 Of course this is always “possible”, but is it considered “offspec”?

 Could/should public space repos be rebroadcastable (ie signed)?

 I’d say public spaces are absolutely different enough to be worth considering special protocol support for. To me public spaces probably exist in two forms: spaces that have always been public and permissioned spaces that turned public. Both of these would benefit from public space commits being rebroadcastable and maybe even being allowed in the firehose/ subscribeRepos semantics. I remember talking about public spaces with @zicklag.dev a whiiiiile back and we kept returning to how loosing out on the firehose is a big big downside to private data that later got made public, but also that permissioned repos later going public is a practically unavoidable usage pattern for many app modalities. I think the sync patterns change enough in these cases that seamlessly integrating with the firehose or something similar is absolutely worth it if you ask me. For the same reasons that not using MSTs and the other existing sync primitives is worth it for permissioned spaces. Not to say it should necessarily be exactly the same primitives as existing public data, but something close to it probably.

There is a bunch here!

 An authenticated endpoint that services (or any identity really) can make calls to to get a list of all spaces that that space host is willing to offer that identity access to to some degree. Could be styled as a spaces version of listReposByCollection.

 I understand the desire for something like this, but there are a few issues with it.

 In the current design, space access is gated primarily by identity of an individual account, and then optionally by app client identity. This means that apps only get access to spaces through an active user session, like an OAuth session. If all app state has been lost, then all those sessions are gone, and the app can’t get access even if they knew to ask.

 A counter-point is that an app service does register as a syncer, and gets notifyWrite pings when any space repo in the space is updated. But that doesn’t include the actual content, and the syncing services needs to authenticate (with a space credential, from a user session) to get the actual data.

 For some applications I think this might be fine. The recovering app will gradually reindex as users log back in and grant access to their space repos, and the app backfills the entire space from the space host. If a user doesn’t re-authenticate, maybe it is good that the service can’t re-index the data?

 I’m not entirely sure how spaces that a user only has read-only access to would be discovered for indexing by the app service. Maybe this becomes modality-specific?

 One thing you can do is backfill all the discoverable “public” spaces (which have declaration records, and will hand out space credentials to anybody).

 On DID document entries:

 I was actually just thinking the opposite today: that we might be able to assume that the space host is always the account host. For individual accounts on a regular PDS with only simplespace , this will be true. And with the “group host” concept, it will also be true for group/community accounts.

 But need to think it through further.

 Public spaces:

 I kind of think it should be possible to tell if a space is re-broadcastable or not should be a permanent status, and indicated in the URI (!).

 A hard direction in particular is a space having been publicly re-broadcast, and then flipped back to non-public.

Some short updates on design progress ( @dholms.xyz can you turn the original post in to a “wiki post”? I think that is just a config flag):

 Public spaces: pretty confident we aren’t going to make any big changes here. No re-distributable cryptographic commitments, no space data on firehoses, repo hosts require space credentials for all space repos (even if “public”). As a small change, will probably update space credential endpoint so that both delegation token and client attestation are optional: that makes it clearer how to fetch “public” spaces w/o an atproto account (if the space authority allows it).

 Repo serialization: expect to ship with STAR files not CAR files

 DPoP: switched to HTTP Message Signatures last week

 Sync scaling/reliability: changes shipped last week

 Cryptographic commitment: think we might need to do proper Diffie-Helman (then KEM for post-quantum). That would mean publishing an addition key in all DID documents but not the end of the world. Also want to iterate on which fields end up in the repo commit metadata object, and which end up as an HTTP header.

 URI scheme: still furiously debating 

 Simplespace configuration: have a thread going over here: Updateable space policy by matthieusieben · Pull Request #119 · bluesky-social/proposals · GitHub , probably should have been a forum thread instead

 Have not started on a couple of the other questions yet. But generally making progress and feels to me like we are on-track to have most of these resolved by end of October, and to be able to ship some time in November.
Yes have made it wiki editable. OP author should be able to do this too FYI.

bnewbold.net: 

 A counter-point is that an app service does register as a syncer

 I was thinking mainly in terms of syncers yes. And services that may have been given long term access directly without access through a user since I expect that will become a somewhat wide spread pattern. But I can also equally see the argument that services will rediscover the spaces they need to know as time goes on and people keep using their clients. Maybe it’s even arguably better if they can’t rediscover without a user in the loop.

 bnewbold.net: 

 I was actually just thinking the opposite today: that we might be able to assume that the space host is always the account host. For individual accounts on a regular PDS with only simplespace , this will be true. And with the “group host” concept, it will also be true for group/community accounts.

 That’s probably fair. The main worry I’d have there is that you might not want to always use simplespace for those cases. But the flip side there is that you can just as well use a custom PDS implementation that implements another space management system.

 My main gripe is I don’t think that we should enforce at a protocol level that a space authority have an account. At least we shouldn’t do that if we continue to make a distinction between space hosts and PDSs, which I think is a worthwhile distinction to make. Lots of space authorities might not need an account. Forcing them to have one when they don’t need it seems a little silly to me.

value.title: A shared lexicon for *video notes*? Looking for input before I build
value.textContent:
I’m considering tobuild an app for recording short screen videos and sharing them as video notes. Basically Loom for AT.

 I’d love your input on the lexicon shape before I settle it.

 The use case 

 You record your screen (a window, a region or the whole display) with your voice and an optional webcam bubble, and share it as a quick explanation, similar to post-it notes or voice memos.

 I see two main user groups: people working together who might send each other video notes (a bug walkthrough, design feedback, a project handover), and educator creators sharing clips with their audience (tutorials, top tips…).

 Why a separate lexicon? 

 These are informal notes, quick to make, and often disposable. They should not appear in the Bluesky video tab, in Bluescreen, or in any other app built for “finished” videos. Promoting a video note to a bsky (or wherever) post is of course possible, but it’s a separate explicit action.

 Visibility 

 Public or unlisted first, private later. Unlisted only means the user’s profile does not list it, because ofc repo data is public. Real private notes will need Spaces. I’d like the record to survive a move into a spaces when that launches.

 Proposed lexicon 

 ( {ns} is a placeholder until there is a name)

 Core (belonging to this app’s domain)

 {ns}.note : the note itself. Might include Title, description, video blob (MP4), thumbnail blob, aspect ratio, duration, capture kind (display, window, region), “listed” flag, timestamps. I like the idea of this maybe being spaced alongside other types of community lexicons for notes (text, voice, image…)

 {ns}.note.defs : any shared definitions such as capture kind and visibility.

 {ns}.comment : a comment on a note, with an optional time anchor in milliseconds and an optional parent for replies. I see bsky posts possibly used here in conjunction but not sure of the implications.

 {ns}.transcript : captions and transcripts, language plus a WebVTT blob, human or automatic.

 {ns}.collection : an ordered set of notes (e.g. for a series, project or course)

 Borrrorws - existing lexicons I’d reuse / connect to interactions:

 Streamplace streams and VODs as source material (similar to how you can create clips from youtube VODs and streams…)

 Bluesky posts as comments

 Scope 

 My MVP scope looks something like this right now: {ns}.note as one record, carrying its own metadata, plus profile reuse and the listed flag. A desktop recorder (Electon), MP4 up to 10 minutes at 720p, uploaded straight to the user’s PDS, within its blob limit.

 Designed for but not built: visibility levels and Spaces, comments, transcripts, collections…

 Out of scope for now: Import Streamplace clips, Post to Bluesky, Bluesky posts as comments.

 What I’d like input on 

 One record or more?

 A neutral community namespace, or an app-level namespace?

 A listed flag now and a visibility enum later: will that survive a move into Spaces?

 Is anyone else already modelling something like this, so we can share / collab?

 —

 Also, different but related topic. I don’t have a name for this yet and I’m not inspired.

 Suggestions welcome across the board!

 Thanks y’all.

Great write up. I’d start with planning for spaces day 1, but you don’t really need to design anything into the lexicon for this I don’t think. That’s an app view / app concern.

 Public vs Unlisted still makes sense too, these are pretty standard patterns.

 I actually don’t think you need a limit? This is another meta item where blob size limits and other parts of the system are going to affect this.

 I probably wouldn’t put collections directly in this lexicon. We don’t have generic collections and it’s a good point: what IS a list of lexicon objects? (That’s not a feed). I guess Semble collections and Grain albums are counter examples.

 Tags are also likely to be useful.

 Comments using rich text and just holding a Bsky post embed could be a thing. And, an app can look for back links without being a comment per se. I think having a first class comment for timeline remarks is good. I’d look at what Leaflet is doing.

 I’m actually a bit confused by just seeing “note” - but I guess you’re leaning on the NS for that. I searched a couple of .video domains and there a bunch that might be relevant.

 I get what you’re thinking about “maybe it’s all notes but they are typed” … but at that point I just want a collection that can hold many different lexicons.

 For Streamplace VODs, I believe it goes beyond blobs to point at external S3 compatible storage - I don’t know how to model this, a blob OR an external link? @iame.li will tell us.

 Other than being adamant that these are “simple” video notes and not important video notes — is there anything here that doesn’t make sense for videos generally? Or is your Loom use case just a way to build an opinionated app that focuses on that style of video?

Hi – I’m working on a transcript format for atproto with Streamplace and Ionosphere, provisionally called TAML (Transcript And Media Layer). You’ve put {ns}.transcript aside for now, so it might be worth a look. Transcripts apply to any video, so one shared lexicon would save each app making its own.

 The text and word timings go in chunk records. A transcript record holds the language and speakers, says how the transcript was made, human or automatic, and points at the video record. WebVTT is generated from the records when a player needs it. For a 10-minute note that’s one transcript record and one chunk. Word timings let you show an interactive transcript or karaoke captions perhaps .

 Corrections and translations are there if you want them later – a correction is a new version, and a translation points back at the version it came from – but you don’t need them to start.

 On Boris’s point about blobs and external storage – the transcript points at the video record, so it doesn’t matter where the video bytes live.

 On comments with a time anchor – if we both count milliseconds from the start of the media, a comment could also point at a range of the transcript text.

 Spec: Transcripts on atproto and MUXL – draft recommendation · GitHub 

Guide: TAML – A Developer's Guide · GitHub 

 The record names are placeholders for now. Happy to talk it through.

value.title: Detecting spaces support
value.textContent:
I’ve been working on a system in HappyView to automatically migrate a user’s spaces data from HappyView to their PDS if I can detect that their PDS supports spaces.

 It’s really hard. 

 describeServer is the first place I checked, but it hasn’t changed in the alpha to indicate support for spaces. The DID document entries for spaces are optional with fallbacks, so we can check for them but their absence doesn’t prove anything.

 My current solution

 This is what I’ve landed on so far, but I’m looking for feedback. Right now, detection is two tiers. First, I check community.lexicon.service.describe . If the server answers it, I treat the method list as authoritative. The presence of spaces XRPCs is a definitive indicator that spaces are supported by the PDS.

 The second tier is required because the reference alpha PDS doesn’t implement community.lexicon.service.describe . Since it’s by far the most common PDS implementation and, thus, the primary target, I fall back to some unreliable status code-based detection:

 Request 
 What the reference PDS says 

 community.lexicon.service.describe 
 400 , not implemented, and notably not a 404 

 com.atproto.space.listSpaces with no auth 
 401 AuthMissing , route present 

 com.atproto.space.<nonexistent> 
 400 InvalidRequest , route absent 

 com.atproto.simplespace.getSpace with no auth 
 400 , route present, rejecting missing params 

 A missing route and a present-but-unparameterised route both return 400 , but an auth-gated method returns 401 . The logic is:

 If we receive the same status code for everything (say all 4 requests return 405 ), we can’t reliably determine spaces support so we assume it isn’t there.

 If we get the expected status codes from each route, we can be reasonably confident that 1) this is a reference PDS, and 2) it has spaces support.

 It’s still a problem

 This method is, to say the least, unreliable. Somebody could be running the reference PDS between a reverse proxy that converts all error responses to 418 just for the memes, meaning the it may support spaces but HV would assume it doesn’t. A non-reference PDS may return the same status codes but have a broken implementation. It’s a minefield.

 Since my survey of the ecosystem shows that it’s safe for now , I’m shipping this detection system today, but I’m hoping there’s a better way. IMHO the ideal would be for the ref PDS to implement community.lexicon.service.describe . Thoughts?
+1 for putting community.lexicon.service.describe support in the reference PDS impl, and if that’s not an available course of action, updating com.atproto.server.describeServer for spaces.

We’ll need to think harder before implementing something like community.lexicon.service.describe on the Bluesky PDS distribution as it’d probably become something of an implicit standard at that point.

 In the mean time & to unblock things, how about just adding a spacesAlpha boolean to the com.atproto.server.describeServer output? (I might not even put it in the lexicon)

 One step further could be experimentalFeatures: ["spaces-alpha"]

Considering the Bluesky PDS is in the minority of PDS implementations that don’t implement community.lexicon.service.describe , I’d say the lexicon has already become an implicit standard.

 Adding a spacesAlpha boolean or an experimentalFeatures array to describeServer certainly works but, like you said, anything added to the reference PDS becomes implicit standard. That ends up being the same as implementing community.lexicon.service.describe .

 I’d wager it’s better to take the time to sort the standard solution for this, rather than jam something in. Besides, I don’t know that anything is blocked right now. I’ve got a hacky solution above that’s working, so we can just roll with that until we have a better idea of how to handle it moving forward.

Following up on @bnewbold.net ’s comment over in the community.lexicon.service.describe thread:

 Working group: service self-description 

 This API came up in a separate thread as being a requirement

 I wanted to make sure it was clear that I’m not demanding the implementation of community.lexicon.service.describe . My goal with this conversation was to find a solution that allows services to detect support for functionality.

 If my reading of the com.atproto.server.describeServer lexicon’s description is correct, it seem like an ideal place for this information:

 Describes the server’s account creation requirements and capabilities.

 Which I’m reading as…

 Describes the server’s account creation requirements AND describes the server’s capabilities.

 …but maybe that’s not the intent.

 Adding spacesAlpha to the com.atproto.server.describeServer schema seems like a band-aid solution to a challenge I expect we’ll run into again as we build more functionality that requires coordination across core atproto infrastructure.

 I think a better long-term solution would be to update describeServer to be more generically expandable, allowing servers to define new functionality without requiring an update to the core com.atproto.* lexicons. For example, an additionalFeatures string array could look like this:

 {
 "properties": {
 "inviteCodeRequired": {},
 "additionalFeatures": {
 "type": "array",
 "description": "A list of features supported by this server.",
 "items": { 
 "type": "string",
 "knownValues": [
 "inviteCodes",
 "emailVerification",
 "phoneVerification",
 "blobUploads",
 "spaces",
 "ssoGoogle",
 "ssoGithub",
 "ssoApple",
 "ssoDiscord"
 ]
 }
 }
 }
}

 Example usage:

 { 
 "inviteCodeRequired": true,
 "additionalFeatures": [
 "spaces",
 "ssoGoogle",
 "ssoGithub",
 "ssoApple",
 "ssoDiscord"
 ]
}

 A open string array also makes it easy for servers to advertise functionality not covered by the core spec (e.g. Tranquil PDS could advertise the SSO items I added above, or the Northsky PDS could advertise Stratos functionality).

IRC prefixes new features with draft- as to distinguish them from the fully ratified form which may have breaking changes from the draft implementation. This is done on live networks, and in my opinion works quite well.

@dholms.xyz @bnewbold.net Have y’all thought anymore about this? I’m closing in on releasing HappyView v3 in the next ~2 weeks, and having a reliable way to detect spaces support would be a huge boon.

Hey thanks for following up!

 Adding spacesAlpha to the com.atproto.server.describeServer schema seems like a band-aid solution to a challenge I expect we’ll run into again

 Yeah it definitely is a bandaid. But I think doing more than that has the potential to become load-bearing before we’ve had time to give it proper thought.

 I’ll ship the spacesAlpha boolean on describeServer next Thursday. That’ll unblock you & other alpha builders. And we can continue wrestling with how/if we want to do feature discovery more generally

How is Standard Site/Leaflet different from RSS?
Leaflet posts and publications are discoverable through RSS. In addition, they are built on top of the Atmosphere using Standard Site.

Standard site is an open publishing protocol, like RSS. It allows compatible readers to syndicate posts and publications. Unlike RSS, it's built on the Atmosphere, allowing it to have associated identity data.

That means that logged in people can subscribe, like, discover, and engage with syndicated posts directly. That new subscription will still belong to the original publication, while meeting the subscriber where they are, dramatically lowering the barrier for discovery and engagement!
Read more about Standard Site here!
How is Leaflet different from Bluesky?

Leaflet and Bluesky are totally separate products built on the Atmosphere. You can think of us as two separate plants in the same soil. We use the same technology, the same accounts system. We integrate with each other and are stronger together. But ultimately we are two different entities.
Leaflet is for Atmospheric newsletters and macroblogging, and Bluesky is for Atmospheric short form microblogging!

Getting started is a quick process, it takes seconds to create a new publication and minutes to publish your first post!

If you've received an invite, check out this tutorial!
Where is my data? Who owns it?
Your data is 100% yours.
It lives in your Atmosphere account. Thats probably the account you made when you signed up to Bluesky. Read more about Atmosphere accounts here!
The data is hosted by whatever service you made your Atmosphere with, again, probably Bluesky. However, Bluesky can't change your data without your explicit permission.

If you don't want Bluesky to host your data, you can move it all to a different Atmosphere account service if you like! Once you move, everything will work exactly the same as it did before. They only thing that will change is where you host your data.
Read more about the Atmosphere here!

What's special about Leaflet

Leaflet is focused on powerful, flexible, and intuitive tooling.
We believe diversity is a pillar of publishing, and we're building a product that can support artists, writers, and creatives in everything they want to accomplish while still being accessible for everyone.

Publications on Leaflet are social. 
When you publish with Leaflet, your post is automatically part of Atmosphere, the same social network that powers Bluesky. That means your work gets syndicated, not just to our reader, but to ALL Atmosphere readers by default. New audiences can discover, subscribe to, and engage with your work from wherever they stumble across it.
Some reader apps you could use include

content.plaintext:
Leaflet Reader
Our in-house reader, convenient and easy to get to. It features an inbox for your subscriptions, as well as new and trending feeds

Pckt Reader
Pckt Blog's reader. It also features an inbox and lots of options to explore trending and popular publications and posts

Standard Reader
A minimal and easy to use Atmospheric reader app that makes it easy to read and search publications

block.plaintext:
Your content and your subscribers are yours. 
They're REALLY yours. The data lives in your Atmosphere Account (that's probably the account you made when your signed up for Bluesky). You can view and manipulate it with a tool like PDSLS.

If you are dissatisfied with us, you don't need to export anything because it's already yours. Just stop using us, and pick an Atmospheric competitor to start using instead. When you log in to that competitor with your Atmosphere account, you content and subscribers will just be there automatically.
How is that possible? It's because we're built on the Atmosphere! Read more about the Atmosphere here!
What does it mean to be "Atmospheric"
It means that Leaflet is powered by the Atmosphere, using Standard Site.
What's the Atmosphere?
The Atmosphere is an ecosystem of social networking apps that all use Atmosphere accounts.

Bluesky is the flagship Atmosphere app. You actually made an Atmosphere account when you signed up for Bluesky! When you sign in to Leaflet (or any other Atmosphere app), you can, and should, use your Bluesky handle, because that's your Atmosphere account!
Atmosphere Accounts are two things!

content.plaintext: A handle, or username.
A big folder, like a Google Drive. Every time you create/like/subscribe/etc on an app, a file is added to your folder recording what you did.

block.plaintext: Atmosphere apps read the files in your folder to show you experiences like a Bluesky feed or a Leaflet publication.
Having many many apps built on top a single huge network of accounts has big advantages for you!

content.plaintext: All the apps share the same log in. How convenient!
The apps integrate well with each other. Leaflet knows who you follow on Bluesky, and Bluesky knows which Leaflet publications belong to you. That makes experience between us as seamless as possible!

block.plaintext: Read more about the Atmosphere here!
What's Standard Site?
Remember that Atmosphere accounts contain a big folder with lots of files that record your activity! Standard site is a type of file in that folder. It's for publications/blogs/newsletters.

Google Docs and Microsoft Word read .docx files. Excel, Numbers and Sheets read .csv files. Leaflet, Pckt, Offprint, and any other newsletter/blogs/readers claiming to be Atmospheric read and/or write Standard Site files.

This standard file type means that can any Standard Site blog can be automatically syndicated to any Atmospheric reader and display nicely. For those used to the online publishing world, the effect is similar to RSS.

Unlike RSS though, Standard Site also allows readers to subscribe and recommend to blogs and blog posts directly from a reader app. This means you can meet people where they are, be discovered via the network, and more easily collect subscriptions.
Read more about Standard Site here!
How is Leaflet different from Substack/Ghost/Buttondown/etc?

Leaflet is a blogging and newsletter tool, like Substack, Ghost and others. We handle publication pages, memberships, email updates, and have a great text editor and interface for drafting and publishing posts.
Substack

Like Substack, Leaflet is easy and intuitive to use. You do not need any technical background at all. We provide tools to layout and theme your publication home page, and an editor to rich posts with lots of rich content like text, images, sub-pages, and embeds.

Also like Substack, Leaflet values the social context your blog lives in. Unlike Substack, we're built on the bustling Atmosphere, the network that Bluesky is built on, with tens of millions of accounts.
Work published on Leaflet automatically syndicates to all Atmosphere readers. And people can discover, subscribe, and engage with posts directly from their reader of choice, like:

content.plaintext: Leaflet Reader
Pckt Reader
Standard Reader

block.plaintext: Of course, in these early days, our network is not yet as robust as Substack’s. But there are real benefits to being an early adopter!
Ghost

Like Ghost, Leaflet is open source, and your data and subscribers belongs entirely to you. We don't own, or even store, your published content or subscribers. We cannot lock you into our app, it's not technically possible. You can leave Leaflet at any time, and you will not need to export your data because we never had it, you do! All that data lives in your Atmosphere Account!
Read more about the Atmosphere here!
What makes Leaflet special
Leaflet has the ease, discovery, and social network of Substack and the openness and ownership of Ghost.

On top of this, Leaflet is committed to powerful and flexible expression. We value diversity, and believe in supporting a rich landscape of publications. We focus on theming, rich content types, and social integrations while still being simple enough for anyone to use!
How does Leaflet integrate with Bluesky?
Leaflet and Bluesky are both apps on the Atmosphere. That means we can easily share data and build lots of integrations. We're always looking for new ways to work together!

Leaflet is built to help creators take advantage of new ways we can make the internet more social, without network lock-in, so you can:

content.plaintext: Publish once and reach readers across Bluesky & beyond

Make money, so your work is sustainable

Share to Bluesky when you publish; Bluesky shows special link cards for Leaflet posts

value.title: What is the Atmosphere?

block.plaintext: Intro and TLDR: What is the Atmosphere
The Atmosphere is an ecosystem of social networking apps that all use Atmosphere accounts so that:

content.plaintext: One account logs you in to all Atmosphere apps
Apps can seamlessly integrate with each other
Apps cannot lock you in and extract you for profit

block.plaintext: Currently, Bluesky is the flagship social network in the Atmosphere but many exist and are growing! Start using any of these today by logging in with your Atmosphere/Bluesky account.
Atmosphere Accounts
Your Atmosphere account (also called a PDS) is:

content.plaintext: Your handle/username
A place that stores the content you create on the apps and the people you have relationships with (follows, followers, mutuals, etc.)

block.plaintext: If you're curious about what this looks like, go to PDSLS and search for your handle. You'll be looking at a big data dump of your content. Click around and you'll see everyone you follow and all the posts, likes, reposts, etc you've ever made on Bluesky!
If you use other Atmosphere apps, those will show up here too!

block.alt: a lil' guy sets up an Atmosphere account. It is depicted as a name tag and a big box of data.

block.plaintext: How do I make an account?
Your Bluesky account IS an Atmosphere account! You can (and should) use it to log into any Atmosphere app!
If you don't want to make your account on Bluesky, you can also create one on some other Atmosphere apps like Tangled, Surf, Blacksky, and Pckt.
A note about your content
You own your account! Not the app you made the account on. Only you can create and change things in it. However, anyone can read and see those things.
Work is being done on private content, but for now think of your content as living in a glass house.
This enables a lot of cool things (which we'll get into), and blocking and moderation tools exist, but it's worth just keeping in mind.

block.alt: a couple lil' guys look through a third lil' guys big box of data

block.plaintext: Why is the Atmosphere so good?
Unified Log In
Once you've made an Atmosphere account, use it for ANY Atmosphere app. It's so convenient!
If you made an account on Bluesky, that's an Atmosphere account. Just use the handle you made there to log into Leaflet, Semble, Tangled, or anywhere else.
Check out this video to see what I mean:
Interoperable apps
All the data is public. That means Atmosphere apps can pull from content from ALL the other apps.

This post is written in Leaflet, a newsletter platform. But I can mention anyone on Bluesky right in line! Look, this is me 
➡️ @cozylittle.house
And in Standard Reader, you can read posts written in not only Leaflet, but other blogging and newsletter platforms like Offprint and Pckt too!
On Bluesky, you'll notice that links to Leaflet, Offprint, and Pckt posts have a fancy special card.
And if you log into Sill, you can see the links and articles that your follows on Bluesky have been posting about.

block.alt: two lil guys with boxes. One is holding the leaflet and pckt logos. Another is handing him the Offprint logo.

block.plaintext: True freedom of choice

Legacy social media companies seem amazing at first, but once they get enough users, it's all about profit extraction. They're no longer making a product in your best interest. You want to leave but they've locked in all your friends and content, so you're stuck. Twitter/X and Instagram stand out as recent examples.

But in the Atmosphere, all your data is public. Let's say an app stops serving you, gets bogged down in ads, changes its algorithm, or supports questionable causes. A competitor will emerge and you can just start using that app instead. Your same content and your same friends, no starting over again. Just totally seamless.
It's already possible today!

content.plaintext: Bluesky is popular, but maybe you'd rather not patron US companies. Or maybe you NEED that edit button. Then use Europe based Mu Social.
Maybe you'd prefer to hear more black voices, in a safe space for black community. Try out Blacksky.
If you want a totally new experience that's mysterious and mindful, maybe Anisota is more for you.

block.plaintext: All your posts, follows, and followers are just there. In fact, give it a try right now. Just log into any of these alternatives with your Atmosphere account. If you don't like them, just head back to Bluesky!

block.alt: two lil guys avoid a pile-of-dog-poop app and instead settle on a nice clean sparkly app.

block.plaintext: Let's sum it up!
The Atmosphere is an ecosystem of apps that use Atmosphere accounts.
An Atmosphere account exists outside of any single app. It consists of a username and a big folder of all the content and relationships a person has. It's public!

Atmosphere apps use this folder to create social experiences like blogging, tweeting, and sharing. Because everything is public, Atmosphere apps can create uniquely seamless experiences between themselves!
Finally, if an app fails to meet your standards, you can always leave the app without leaving your connections and your content.
The Atmosphere! Greener pastures await!

block.alt: a lil' guy finds himself surrounded by options now that they're on the Atmosphere!

value.title: What is Standard Site, and why is it useful?

block.alt: Three lil' guys gather around a standard site logo with wires coming out of it. The guys appear to be connecting the wires to something

block.plaintext: Standard Site, launched at the beginning of this year, is a set of shared standards for publishing longform content on the internet, focused on interoperable content discovery and social features.
As the @standard.site ecosystem grows — from Bluesky's link card integration to WordPress's new plugin to community reader tools emerging — more people are hearing about it and wondering:
What exactly is Standard Site, and what is it good for?
TL;DR what is Standard Site?
The easiest way to think about Standard Site is probably:
What if we had a way to write and follow publications on the internet, built on a large-scale social network graph?
It's a standard format for publishing and engaging with longform content on the internet (think: blogs!) in a way that's linked to your identity and easy to aggregate, built on AT Protocol.
Here's what happens when you publish something using Standard Site — a blog post in a Leaflet publication, for example:

features.contentPlaintext:
Records belong to different Lexicons, which is how atproto defines structured data schemas.

In Standard Site, things like publications, posts (documents), and subscriptions are each different record types.
Personal Data Store — this is where your atproto data lives; it can be hosted anywhere, but it's always under your account's control.

content.plaintext: a record* for the post is published to your PDS*

features.contentPlaintext: Apps listen to the firehose, a stream of all new data published on the network, then filter and cache in AppViews specific to their needs. The protocol ensures that all data is verifiably what each identity actually published.

content.plaintext: this shows up on the public firehose* — a source for distribution that's really easy for others to build on
services can crawl and index this data in different ways and do all sorts of cool things with it, like aggregate it for readers

features.contentPlaintext: In atproto this is your DID (Decentralized Identifier), a stable ID that maps to your handle. You can change your handle but your DID stays the same.

content.plaintext: all this is associated with your identity*, stable across the network

block.plaintext: Writers: posts you publish live in a place you control. Readers: your subscriptions and recommends do too.
Per @jimray.bsky.team in Let’s build an Atmospheric Web, it's about enabling both ownership and distribution in the social web.
How is this different from RSS?
The basic problem RSS solves: given a blog (or podcast / website), what are its latest posts?

Standard Site is also about aggregating longform content on the internet. The two biggest differences are that with Standard Site, data is fundamentally associated with identity, and it's easy to index across the entire network.

With social primitives in Standard Site that don't exist in RSS, like recommends and subscribes, together with user identity, we can build up a really useful graph of social relationships around content. This makes it easy to, for example, see all the publications your friends subscribe to, or what posts they've most shared.
With the atproto firehose, we get a global distribution layer, compared to RSS where crawling and collection is more ad-hoc.
Jim also describes how atproto and RSS complement one another, and how new feed readers might enable richer social experiences, at What you can do with AT Protocol.
What Standard Site makes possible
Standard Site enables more flexible, composable experiences for readers and writers alike; lots of cool things are possible already:

content.plaintext: Your posts and publications can be discoverable in reader tools and filterable based on your social graph
In an app like Leaflet, you can see all the Bluesky conversations that link to a given blog post
People can subscribe to publications with their atproto account, as an alternative to email — and because subs are public, you can sign into any reader app and they'll be there

block.plaintext: Different apps can compete on different parts of the experience, and things like this become possible in Bluesky — or in any app:

As Standard Site becomes more ubiquitous, we get something like RSS but with full social context, including two-way relationships between readers and publishers, as well as exciting potential for things like communities within the broader social graph.

Readers get stronger signals for discovery and more ways to enter conversations. Publishers get stronger connections to their audience and more flexibility with things like memberships. For example, we could build ways to let your Bluesky followers get exclusive access to certain content, or members-only commenting permissions.
How do I use Standard Site?
You can publish with @leaflet.pub — or other tools like @pckt.blog and @offprint.app — to publish to Standard Site out of the box.
If you have a self-hosted static site you can use @sequoia.pub to easily publish Standard Site records, or roll your own integration.
On WordPress? Use the ATmosphere plugin or Autoblue.
There are a few layers to how you can use Standard Site — you can use all of these, or just some:

content.plaintext: metadata layer: basic info like publication name, post titles, publication date, author, etc; useful for interop with various discovery and reader tools; most RSS-like
content layer: the actual content you're publishing, which can be in any format; not required, but putting this on protocol enables things like richer search and backlinks
social layer: things like subscriptions (to a publication) and recommendations (of a post), linked to your identity

block.plaintext: To explore the ecosystem, check out:

content.plaintext: reader apps like @skyreader.app or @standard-reader.app
pub search to query across Standard Site posts
someone even made a TUI reader!

block.plaintext: Standard Site is a great example of what AT Protocol makes possible as a technology, and what the Atmosphere makes possible as an ecosystem — a collaboratively created and stewarded set of standards leading to the emergence of lots of useful things.
It's not just a theoretical spec but a pragmatic thing that's easy to integrate, and already being widely implemented.
Play around, explore the docs, and reach out if you have questions!

content.plaintext: Who owns the published posts?
The publication creator — posts live in their PDS
Any submission / approval flow?
No, it's simple for now, collaborators can publish directly
Can I invite a contributor just to a single post?

Not yet; once someone's a publication contributor you can add them to a per-post byline, but can't add someone for a single guest post; any contributor can make and publish new posts so this is best for trusted collaborators for now

If the pub owner is authed in Leaflet this should Just Work! If their session is expired or they've logged out, they'll need to log in again first.

block.plaintext: In the very early days of the atmosphere we only had Smoke Signal. Made by @ngerakines.me it clearly demonstrated how events could  work on the atmosphere, complete with an open events lexicon for subsequent apps to hop on to.

Whereas Nick had replicated the essence of Luma, @tompscanlan.bsky.social needed a Meetup alternative and built one accordingly. Since there were no private spaces on the horizon back in 2025, OpenMeet started out very bespoke, gradually aligning more closely with the AT protocol as it matured.

features.contentPlaintext: as afforded to it by Smoke Signal's prior art❣️

block.plaintext: Then came atmo.rsvp by flo-bit.dev. Another Luma-like, but with more of a design-first approach*; an instant hit among the atproto nerds.
For the past year I've been intermittently checking in with all the aforementioned project owners to advocate for a more intentionally coordinated events stack in the atmosphere.

block.alt:
From Erlend to Tom on Discord:
I believe you, flo, Nick and a handful others want 90% the same thing in an events app. That's enough overlap that it really makes far more economic/social sense to make one bigger app together, and then in theory the difference in preferences could be made up for by user configuration and mini-app-offshoots for bespoke features.
the atmosphere makes that kind of story far more plausible, since by all building on the same protocol you're in a large sense already building the same app, just with slightly different views.

block.plaintext: Everyone in the bunch has been positively inclined since the start, but these things take time. The hardest thing about making this sort of collaboration happen is deciding whose codebase to rally around, since each developer is naturally most comfortable and attached to their own work which they know intimately.
Longer story short though, convergence is now happening! Smoke Signal has been simplified to a read-only events browser, deferring to atmo.rsvp and OpenMeet for actual scheduling.

As for OpenMeet, Tom has very graciously agreed to incrementally transition the very sizable amount of work he put into OpenMeet over to atmo.rsvp (or atmo-events as the code repo is called), essentially merging the two apps together.

It's a massive win-win: OpenMeet gets a more streamlined interface while atmo-events gets extended with a bunch of Meetup-like organizational features. openmeet.net may continue operations to service its existing userbase, but as another instance of atmo-events as opposed to a separately maintained codebase.

features.contentPlaintext: tbd, but that's what I'm advocating for and feels like a natural progression.

block.plaintext: Tom and Florian have already been co-authoring atmo-events and contrail (its appview) for several months. Now that these are no longer single-person projects those repos will likely be moved into organizational management* to further facilitate communal ownership of the canonical atmospheric events stack.
I see this partnership as emblematic of the "Atmospheric Stacks" model we're seeing organically take shape for every major application archetype.
Make events better for everyone

atmo-events isn't a single website, it's atmospheric-events-in-a-box. Events are an inherently local phenomenon and as such they tend to work best as bespoke websites rooted in place, like the Danish activist calendar dukop.dk .

What local organizers don't want is having to choose between several small indie projects with uncertain futures, all seemingly trying to solve the same problems but in subtly different ways, making it very hard to pick the Right One to get the job done.
By building events as a community-powered stack we can rally around the essential affordances for events organizing and leave the finer details to the localized implementations.

value.title: Making software hurts now

block.plaintext: American Monorail weave room, Elrod Collection – Greenville Historical Society

Making open source software used to be among the least controversial acts imaginable. The worst that could happen when you freely shared your work with the world was that no one cared. And if just one person did care enough to even say so, it was connection, it was community, it was everything.
Sharing truly was caring; for one's own development, for the receiver's enjoyment, and for the quality of the code.

Now, every act of giving is treated with suspicion. The gift of openness is no longer trustworthy on its own. The receivers of free software want to know how the gift came to be. Is it pure, or was it made with dirty machinery?

In the case of the latter, some especially angry, would-be recipients won't just ignore the giver and forego the gift, they'll attack the giver with the fervor of someone who has themselves been attacked, apparently by the voluntary offer on hand.

The anger is justified, but the target is tragically misguided, and it is fracturing the software developer community at a time when solidarity is the only way our technology will be ours to wield again.
There is no opting out
The tech we make more tech with is chiefly chosen for us, not by us.

features.contentPlaintext: the role is not the issue, the disproportionate volume is.

block.plaintext: Fewer industries are better at manufacturing demand than the devtools industry. When the corporate world wants a new technology adopted they have an army of marketers and good DevRel* soldiers they'll send out to make the latest addition to the stack self-evident; the missing piece you didn't know you needed!
And two things can be true at once: The new thing wouldn't have risen to prominence the way it did without major financial backing, but it was also plain good tech with real utility.

Software developers prize their autonomy and are quick to judge peers who don't exercise their agency enough to leave that shitty company or drop that antiquated framework. But devs operate under the laws of economic realities just like the rest of the working class, and many have learned in recent years just how little power we workers actually have to protect ourselves when the jobs market is shrinking.

Suddenly, opting not to do React because "it doesn't suit my sensibilities as a developer" isn't a position you can afford to hold any longer, no more than the weaver artisans could afford to say no to a job at the factory.

features.contentPlaintext: and the ones who really scare me have done so aggressively.

block.plaintext: So too with AI. Yes there were the early adopters who embraced it eagerly*, but far more have reluctantly come along for the ride simply because the industry decided this is how we do things now. Many probably even believe they were willing adopters, but really it's just a story they tell themselves as they cling to a fading sense of agency in their craft.

If you've opted out you're one of the lucky, privileged few that the ruthless march of industry hasn't conscripted yet. But don't conflate your enviable happenstance with a stronger backbone than your peers. I ask that you be more compassionate, for we are all cognizant of our entrapment and are working our way out of it as best we know how.
AI erodes trust

features.contentPlaintext: aka glue work.

block.plaintext: As an "open source social worker"*, I perceive the greatest cost of AI to be the erosion of trust among open software practitioners. It has utterly upended our gift economy, turning well meaning developers against each other in a cold civil war beset with spy games.

No one is safe. Speak about your use of AI in a side project and your community might shun you. Speak ill of AI and your employer might fire you. To practice open software now is to practice great caution at every turn. Every utterance about software needs to be qualified with a position, a declaration of allegiance or inoffensive ambivalence.

The community of practice that I've grown up with, played with, and built with is eating itself from the inside. It hurts. We're all hurting so bad that every few weeks there's a new announcement of a cherished peer leaving tech to save their sanity.
I feel like a weary old man reading the obituaries of people I used to know from the neighborhood, and find myself wondering how long until I join them.

I don't know how much time my waning tech career has got left in it, but I do know I'm done wasting any more of it being judgemental and angry at my fellow makers of public goods. Factory-made or not, I'm grateful for every gift I'm given.
