value.title: Technorealists, the silent majority?

block.plaintext: Centrism is most widely understood to be a political stance between two extremes a left-to-right polarity. It can serve a useful role, especally in multi-party systems where the centrists represent a spectrum of real political platforms rather than the inneffectual  bothsidesing it amounts to in the binary system of the USA.

It's an especially aggravating stance when the two extremes aren't so much political as they are existential. On the one hand we've got a global elite of business-as-usual conglomerates hellbent on growing for growth's sake until something pops so bad it'll ring our ears for generations to come.

Meanwhile the global majority agrees we desperately need systems change, but we're still figuring out exactly what that ought to look like and how we can possibly wrest enough power away from the CEO-class to implement said changes.
Cue the centrist coming in to say both sides are taking it too far and the status-quo is not that bad actually, it just needs a few incremental tweaks, from fascism to not-quite-so-much fascism.

features.contentPlaintext: More of this metaphor in JD's Traditional Social Media as a Prison.

block.plaintext: There's no left or right to quibble about here. There are 3500 prison owners and 8.3 billion of us living inside their walls*.
Social media hates a centrist

Western social media in particular has been shaped in the mold of US two-party politics, so the centrist position is tantamount to "voting independent", which is how you draw the ire of 99% of the population instead of just the "opposing" other half.

In the painfully limiting context of American political discourse this aversion to the middle ground is appropriate, but applied generally it's dysfunctional. Cars have their uses, and so do bikes. Most people share the centrist position that both modes of transport serve a legitimate purpose.

But social media thrives on extremes. That's where outrage happens, driving clicks and impressions. You'll never hear from the people in the middle because their opinions are boringly sensible and uncontroversial.
Spiritually centered
Many wisdom traditions consider centrism - that is, to be mindfully centered - nothing less than the path to enlightenment.

The Middle Way refers to a spiritual practice that steers clear of both extreme asceticism and sensual indulgence.

The second formulation, "teaching the Dharma by the middle," refers to how the Buddha's Dharma (Teaching) approaches ontological issues of existence and personal identity by avoiding eternalism (or absolutism) and annihilationism (or nihilism).

Our collective failure to live these teachings hit me flat in the face every day as I open my social feed and do my best to mentally filter out the incessant arguing between technological boosters and doomers.

Neither group will readily agree with that derogatory labeling, but they have nonetheless picked a tribal side in what their social media feed of outrage porn paints as a simple binary. Everything they hear about "the other side" is the most extreme example.

content.plaintext: "There's no such thing as a good data center" vs "If you like the internet you have to like data centers"
"AI isn't good for anything" vs "AI is the best thing ever and it's gonna be 10x better by next year"
"All money is rooted in evil" vs "Capitalism is the only practical coordination-mechanism we've got; there is no alternative."

block.plaintext: None of this is representative of common sense in the wider populace; the common ground that's invariably surfaced by having a good-faith conversation for more than 10 minutes. Once you get past the rapid-fire soundbites into "oh sure, if you put it (sensibly, boringly) like that"-territory, the middle way prevails more often than not.
Common sense majority
Most people don't actually hate data centers as a whole, they just object to them being built everywhere all at once against the popular will of directly affected locals.
Most people don't want to take your coding agent away, they just want their google searches to return actual websites again.
Most people understand the value of businesses, but they're fed up with the repeated overreach of big business that have long since stopped playing by the rules all the rest of us are bound by.

Yes, AI has an increasing number of legitimate uses, especially and unsurprisingly in the STEM field from which it originated. And yes, AI is the product of a dominator culture that has yet to properly reckon with its anti-social origins and internal programming premised on extraction. Both are true, and neither can be properly understood in denial of the other.

The extent to which our latest technological innovation works isn't the real point of contention. What the critics worry about is a naive adherence to technological advancement in a time when technology is chiefly wielded by an undemocratic, unelected minority of god-kings whose grand vision for this technology is to make themselves so powerful as to become ungovernable.
You might be a technorealist

I first drafted this article thinking what I was talking about would be called 'technological centrism', but apparently the term technocentrism has already been coined to mean something more akin to techno-solutionism.
Turns out the term I was reaching for is technorealism, introduced in the 90s by technosocial luminaries like Douglass Rushkoff, admittedly one of my most beloved living influences.

Technorealism is an attempt to expand the middle ground between techno-utopianism and Neo-Luddism by assessing the social and political implications of technologies so that people might all have more control over the shape of their future.

[the goal was] not to promote or dismiss technology but to understand it so the application could be aligned with basic human values. Technorealism suggests that a technology, however revolutionary it may seem, remains a continuation of similar revolutions throughout human history.
The technorealist manifesto hasn't survived the unrelenting entropy of link rot, but you can read the whole thing here:
Its central argument reads as if it was written yesterday.

In this heady age of rapid technological change, we all struggle to maintain our bearings. The developments that unfold each day in communications and computing can be thrilling and disorienting. One understandable reaction is to wonder: Are these changes good or bad? Should we welcome or fear them?

The answer is both. Technology is making life more convenient and enjoyable, and many of us healthier, wealthier, and wiser. But it is also affecting work, family, and the economy in unpredictable ways, introducing new forms of tension and distraction, and posing new threats to the cohesion of our physical communities.
That was 30 years ago, talking about the unstoppable march of a mystifying new technology called the internet.

It was always just a matter of time until the sum of all human knowledge would be put onto a supercomputer and become a pseudo-sentient library of everything. But there was nothing inevitable about who would own, direct and benefit the most from the internet's societal disruption, nor who it would externalize its harms to.

Perhaps with hindsight we can say it was only ever gonna go the way of the internet oligarchy we're now beset with, but that same hindsight can bestow upon us a clearsightedness we lacked in the last millennium. We played the tape and now we're living the world that inaction between fictitious opposites leads to.

There's another way to go about this. Not to the left nor the right, but a middle way in between; a way of expanding the middle ground so as to see ourselves where most of us are actually standing: in the unremarkable center.
Technorealist manifesto

In this heady age of rapid technological change, we all struggle to maintain our bearings. The developments that unfold each day in communications and computing can be thrilling and disorienting. One understandable reaction is to wonder: Are these changes good or bad? Should we welcome or fear them?

The answer is both. Technology is making life more convenient and enjoyable, and many of us healthier, wealthier, and wiser. But it is also affecting work, family, and the economy in unpredictable ways, introducing new forms of tension and distraction, and posing new threats to the cohesion of our physical communities.

Despite the complicated and often contradictory implications of technology, the conventional wisdom is woefully simplistic. Pundits, politicians, and self-appointed visionaries do us a disservice when they try to reduce these complexities to breathless tales of either high-tech doom or cyber-elation. Such polarized thinking leads to dashed hopes and unnecessary anxiety, and prevents us from understanding our own culture.

Over the past few years, even as the debate over technology has been dominated by the louder voices at the extremes, a new, more balanced consensus has quietly taken shape. This document seeks to articulate some of the shared beliefs behind that consensus, which we have come to call technorealism.

Technorealism demands that we think critically about the role that tools and interfaces play in human evolution and everyday life. Integral to this perspective is our understanding that the current tide of technological transformation, while important and powerful, is actually a continuation of waves of change that have taken place throughout history. Looking, for example, at the history of the automobile, television, or the telephone -- not just the devices but the institutions they became -- we see profound benefits as well as substantial costs. Similarly, we anticipate mixed blessings from today's emerging technologies, and expect to forever be on guard for unexpected consequences -- which must be addressed by thoughtful design and appropriate use.

As technorealists, we seek to expand the fertile middle ground between techno-utopianism and neo-Luddism. We are technology "critics" in the same way, and for the same reasons, that others are food critics, art critics, or literary critics. We can be passionately optimistic about some technologies, skeptical and disdainful of others. Still, our goal is neither to champion nor dismiss technology, but rather to understand it and apply it in a manner more consistent with basic human values.
Below are some evolving basic principles that help explain technorealism.
Principles of Technorealism
1. Technologies are not neutral.
2. The Internet is revolutionary, but not Utopian.

The Net is an extraordinary communications tool that provides a range of new opportunities for people, communities, businesses, and government. Yet as cyberspace becomes more populated, it increasingly resembles society at large, in all its complexity. For every empowering or enlightening aspect of the wired life, there will also be dimensions that are malicious, perverse, or rather ordinary.
3. Government has an important role to play on the electronic frontier.

Contrary to some claims, cyberspace is not formally a place or jurisdiction separate from Earth. While governments should respect the rules and customs that have arisen in cyberspace, and should not stifle this new world with inefficient regulation or censorship, it is foolish to say that the public has no sovereignty over what an errant citizen or fraudulent corporation does online. As the representative of the people and the guardian of democratic values, the state has the right and responsibility to help integrate cyberspace and conventional society.

Technology standards and privacy issues, for example, are too important to be entrusted to the marketplace alone. Competing software firms have little interest in preserving the open standards that are essential to a fully functioning interactive network. Markets encourage innovation, but they do not necessarily insure the public interest.
4. Information is not knowledge.

All around us, information is moving faster and becoming cheaper to acquire, and the benefits are manifest. That said, the proliferation of data is also a serious challenge, requiring new measures of human discipline and skepticism. We must not confuse the thrill of acquiring or distributing information quickly with the more daunting task of converting it into knowledge and wisdom. Regardless of how advanced our computers become, we should never use them as a substitute for our own basic cognitive skills of awareness, perception, reasoning, and judgment.
5. Wiring the schools will not save them.

The problems with America's public schools -- disparate funding, social promotion, bloated class size, crumbling infrastructure, lack of standards -- have almost nothing to do with technology. Consequently, no amount of technology will lead to the educational revolution prophesied by President Clinton and others. The art of teaching cannot be replicated by computers, the Net, or by "distance learning." These tools can, of course, augment an already high-quality educational experience. But to rely on them as any sort of panacea would be a costly mistake.
6. Information wants to be protected.

It's true that cyberspace and other recent developments are challenging our copyright laws and frameworks for protecting intellectual property. The answer, though, is not to scrap existing statutes and principles. Instead, we must update old laws and interpretations so that information receives roughly the same protection it did in the context of old media. The goal is the same: to give authors sufficient control over their work so that they have an incentive to create, while maintaining the right of the public to make fair use of that information. In neither context does information want "to be free." Rather, it needs to be protected.
7. The public owns the airwaves; the public should benefit from their use.

The recent digital spectrum giveaway to broadcasters underscores the corrupt and inefficient misuse of public resources in the arena of technology. The citizenry should benefit and profit from the use of public frequencies, and should retain a portion of the spectrum for educational, cultural, and public access uses. We should demand more for private use of public property.
8. Understanding technology should be an essential component of global citizenship.

In a world driven by the flow of information, the interfaces -- and the underlying code -- that make information visible are becoming enormously powerful social forces. Understanding their strengths and limitations, and even participating in the creation of better tools, should be an important part of being an involved citizen. These tools affect our lives as much as laws do, and we should subject them to a similar democratic scrutiny.

Any and all threads I'm following from across the entire atmosphere, ordered chronologically by latest activity. These are the persistent threads that I have a vested interest in moving continuously forward, albeit asynchronously and never all at once.

value.title: The Atmosphere, Explained

block.plaintext: A new internet is being built atop a modern web commons called the atmosphere.

It's a pro-social reimagining of the digital world most of us know today as a dismal status quo of monopolistic data enclosures. So severely has the well been poisoned that the mere mention of "social media" makes us sick to our stomachs.
Unlike the platform-mediated internet that designs for attention-capture, a genuinely social internet designs for agency, instilled in persons and communities alike.

The new internet isn't coming soon, it's a present reality comprising hundreds of social applications interoperating with one another as one network. 45 million of us have already left the old world, now directing our liberated attentions toward a digital sphere of our own making.
The Old
What we leave behind.

The monopolized web as we know it enforces a tight coupling of platform and user-data, effectively keeping users captive and pitting the platforms against each other in a zero-sum game of "who can claim the most users".

block.alt: Facebook, Twitter and Discord represented as closed-system silos.

block.plaintext: You can set up simultaneous residence in all these platforms, but your identity and the data it's comprised of may not travel freely between them. What happens in Facebook stays in Facebook.
This leaves our online identity in a perpetual state of fragmentation as we string a mishmash of competing platforms together to establish some semblance of a unified digital expression.
The New
Personal data ownership begets collective power.
The latest iteration of the social internet builds on emerging web standards that separate user data from the platform. This decoupling has major implications for the individual web user's agency.

block.alt: Platform on one side, Data/ID on the other, with a thin line separating them.

block.plaintext: Once your data is no longer tightly coupled with your social media app of choice, that platform becomes a mere custodian of your data as opposed to being the owner of it, the same way a bank keeps your money safe on your behalf but it doesn't strictly control your use of it.

features.contentPlaintext: and as evidenced by the AM/FM hybrid, the AT protocol might later exist in conjunction with other protocols that solve the same problems with a different technical implementation.

block.plaintext: Every application in the atmosphere-net builds atop the same standard, technically called the AT protocol or atproto for short. What the AT stands for is no more important than the AM/FM* protocols that make your radio work, or the SMS you send to that friend who (justifiably) refuses to install WhatsApp.
What matters is what this standard of interoperability affords us as netizens.
Nomadic homesteading
Digital agency as akin to home ownership.

features.contentPlaintext: in the physical world I live in one of these and I quite like it! But on the web where I have the ability to teleport, a static apartment is too constrictive.

block.plaintext: Instead of renting personal data-space in a rigid apartment complex*, in the atmospheric model we each get a campervan for our data.
This makes every application a mere entrypoint to the wider network. The network, the atmosphere, extends far beyond the application-bound borders of any single platform.

block.alt: Large cluster of people (as avatars) in the center, surrounded by platforms that all feed into the same network of people.

block.plaintext: Not every app is a data-host. Many not listed here opt instead to defer account-hosting to a bigger provider like Bluesky or Eurosky.

Whichever atmospheric social app you start out on will grant you a virtual campervan - a storage-space of personal data - that's yours for life. With it you're free to traverse the atmosphere in its entirety.
Freedom of movement across the world-wide web
Signed up for Bluesky? You'll begin your journey as @alice.bsky.social, like a van that comes with a bit of promotional branding on the side.

block.plaintext: Some guy called  Dean Ball said
Open-weight models are inherently decelerationist
This other guy called Nathan Lambert says he’s right

Open models are decelerationist economically for the frontier labs, which will slow the net investment and capex rollout for AI. This is due to the fact that strong open-weight AI models massively reduce the margin potential for the closed labs. This has two effects. These together will slow timelines to the most transformative AI models

block.plaintext: To no one’s surprise except the valley-brained, open models are indeed the way. Just open-weight models for now, but that’s enough of a crack for the light to get in*.

block.plaintext: Thinking more about what a social media experience made for social cohesion could look like, I was reminded of a paper by E. Glen Weyl, Audrey Tang and others* called Community by Design, subsequently published as a more easily digestible article.

block.title: Building A Prosocial Media Ecosystem | NOEMA
block.description: There’s never been a better time to make social media what it always should have been: a tool to strengthen rather than strip-mine the social fabric.

block.plaintext: It centers around the concept of social bridging, a way of interconnecting and ranking content for the purpose of bridging social divides as opposed to exacerbating them for the purpose of outrage and clicks.
Audrey Tang frames this as discovering our 'uncommon ground'.

“Plurality is about a diffusion of diverse viewpoints. Through technology, we have a way to discover our uncommon ground so that even though we come from different places, there’s a systemic way to co-create policies and norms,” Tang said. By “uncommon ground,” she means those rare points of agreement that people with very different ideological views often don’t realise they share — values that can be uncovered through deep listening and mutual understanding, creating space to move beyond polarisation.
An aside on advertising

The 'Community by Design' paper outlines several prospective interventions, including a complete overhaul of the advertising business model with the aim of putting those ad dollars in service of social cohesion.

While I'd personally like to leave most forms of advertising behind us as we move on to a new and better web, @robin.berjon.com & friends in the Modal foundation happen to be among the very few people who could get it right.

That said, I don't think we're ready for that discussion yet, as its largely contingent on whatever Bluesky decides to do first with its 99% market share of the Atmosphere's attention economy. There's no meaningful leverage there for smaller players until the collective pie has grown by an order of magnitude.
Community Notes
The lowest-hanging fruit bridge available to us appears to be the community-powered sensemaking utility popularized on Twitter called Community Notes.

It pursues social bridging by means of contextualizing potentially misleading posts with crowd-sourced addendums. The system is not without its challenges, but no system of democratization ever is. It can only be improved by engaging with it.

What makes Community Notes such an easy win for the open social web is that most of the design work is already done by @jonathanwarden.com who's been "working on algorithms to make online conversations less toxic and more intelligent" for many, many years.

block.plaintext: IndieAuth
Nearing a decade ago, @aaronpk.com made a compelling case for IndieAuth, a "decentralized identity protocol built on top of OAuth".

block.title: OAuth for the Open Web
block.description: OAuth has become the de facto standard for authorization and authentication on the web. Nearly every company with an API used by third party developers has implemented OAuth to enable people to build apps on top of it.

block.plaintext: OAuth has become the de facto standard for authorization and authentication on the web. Nearly every company with an API used by third party developers has implemented OAuth to enable people to build apps on top of it.
While OAuth is a great framework for this, the way it has ended up being used is much more centralized and closed than prior efforts

Instead of social-web platforms defaulting to the single sign-on hegemony of Google/Facebook/Microsoft(GitHub) as the only options for quick sign-in, what if there was one universal field where all auth providers were equals?
IndieAuth, built as an extension of the ubiquitous OAuth standard, lets you login with your website.
This evens the playing field, genuniely democratizing OAuth as the universal method of internet login.
Unfortunately it never made it to mainstream adoption. No matter how universal, single-field-of-text just can't compete with single-button-click.
The only way to solve for that is in the browser.
FedCM

A lot can be said about the maligned incentives of Big Browser incumbents to maintain their comfortable status quo and why it's taken a decade for tangible progress to be made on this end, but instead of dwelling on the past we can look to the future that is the FedCM standard:

block.title: FedCM: A privacy-preserving identity federation API  |  Identity  |  Chrome for Developers
block.description: A web platform API that allows users to login to websites with their federated accounts in a manner compatible with improvements to browser privacy.

block.plaintext: FedCM, developed by @sgo.to & co., turns the finicky text-entry into a streamlined button-click (auto-click even) by keeping your default website-logins stored for you.
Presently this only works in Chrome browsers (then again that's like 65%-75% of all netizens already), but the rest are coming along.
This will be further helped on by the Bluesky-funded work on FedCM being done by @thisismissem.social to align it with the open-social web.
update:
Follow the development of the IdP Registration API.
Atmospheric OAuth
The AT protocol had to develop a more decentralized alternative to OIDC in order to fit atproto's open-social identity system onto OAuth.
The result was the atproto-oauth spec.
CIMD
@atproto/oauth-provider diverges from OIDC by supporting CIMD, which is essential to auth flows like that of IndieAuth.
Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) let OAuth clients identify themselves using a URL. No preregistration necessary.
DID:PLC
It's also compatible with atproto-identities, which grants users of atmospheric apps the critical affordance of credible-exit. The did:plc method is what makes this possible.

features.contentPlaintext: Formal association has been founded, but now official announcement yet.

block.plaintext: It's a centralized registry, but it's easily replicable and held in a non-profit foundation*. There's even a clear path towards greater decentralization in the future, it's just not an urgent need given how reasonably anti-fragile the system already is.
With all of the above combined with FedCM we get a web-wide login experience that rivals the hegemons.
We have users knocking on our doors: let’s give them a best in class first impression of the Atmosphere and set them up for their next run-ins with us.
I believe there are really just two key components to set us on our way to Web future.
A recognizable login button. When users see it they know they can login with their Atmosphere account. And they will come to expect an Atmospheric experience once they’re in.

An account picker that feels like it comes with you across the Atmosphere. If a user already has an Atmosphere account, they should be no more than three clicks away from using your app once they discover it.
A web OS grounded in identity

In a powerful demonstration of what this new bundle of identity standards affords us, @scottlanoue.com has functionally prototyped atmospheric accounts working on-device, thus completely supplanting the native account systems of Android and iOS.
IndieAuth v2 is already here
As a participant in the atmospheric web I am already enjoying the  "IndieAuth v2" experience, made up of atproto-oauth, FedCM and did:plc.

block.plaintext: What's been achieved with AT protocol identities is arguably not very far off from the essence of the old WebID* either. For the end-user it's functionally doing the same sort of thing:
WebID-based protocols offer a new way to log into internet services. Instead of using a password, the member refers to another web address which can vouch for it.

I'm just throwing that out there because in my humble opinion the general (O)Auth & (D)ID pattern outlined by the AT protocol is what I've always wanted as my personal web ID, and I think most internet users would agree if they could share in my experience.
This doesn't need to be an atproto thing. It's an OAuth and DIDs thing. Other protocols can introduce alternative, even cooler DID methods than the Atmosphere's PLC.

The easiest way to supersede the did:plc whilst benefiting from its ecosystem is to follow the pattern of did:plc:bft which simultaneously acts as a mirror and an alt-method with additional, even more decentralized capabilities.

From a foundational point of view, didplcbft is designed to operate independently from plc.directory, such that it could eventually replace it, becoming the de facto PLC service. However, as a transitional approach, didplcbft can act as more of a mirror of an authoritative PLC implementation, namely, plc.directory.
This is how other networks like ActivityPub and Matrix could hop on the DIDs bandwagon without being beholden to atproto infrastructure.
Distributed identity across the social web
There was recently a great convening of social-web stewards from across nations and protocols.

block.title: The European Social Stack · An open declaration
block.description: An open declaration: The European Social Stack. Open Social Platforms and Private Messaging.

block.plaintext: One section commits the signatories to a common identity stack.
What the signatories intend to build together.
The development of a system for a distributed identity that can be used across networks and beyond (e.g. the European Digital ID Wallet) and protects personal data.
The IndieAuth/WebID-like pattern is another such distributed identity system that can be used across networks, and in a much more global and neutral way than EUID.

For ActivityPub this pattern has largely been proven out already in NomadPub, which includes support for did:plc. Furthermore CIMD is making its way into Doorkeeper, which is upstream of OAuth in Mastodon. The ActivityPub API Task Force has also expressed interest in the aforementioned IdP Registration API.
Matrix implements OIDC, it just needs to additionally adopt the OAuth-DID pattern as a blessed form of decentralized user accounts.
With FedCM, OAuth and DIDs as the unifiers, we wouldn't have to talk about logging in with "atmosphere / bluesky / mastodon / fediverse / web3"; just log in with your Open Social Web Identity.

value.title: Energy Realism

block.plaintext: So this was posted yesterday
and my heart sank a bit seeing how excitedly this hyperbole was received by many peers in my corner of the social web.
I have no beef with @squarelyrooted.bsky.social; every well-intentioned optimist is a friend of mine, and I don't think they intended their statement to go viral like that.

But since it did, and because it seemed to resonate so strongly with a significant number of people, I gotta say my piece. This is merely a retort to the statement, not the person, it just doesn't feel right to paste in an "anonymized" screenshot when we can sense-make together with backlinks.
My response won't be as quippy and it'll take 5 minutes to read, so its odds of reaching a comensurate amount of people are slim.
Still, someone is wrong on the internet and the record needs correcting.
It's this statement in particular that is misleadingly hyperbolic:
we're turbodeploying unlimited free energy

The growth of solar and the other renewables is incredible and I'm here for it, but we just can't go around saying "free, unlimited energy" like that's something we can look forward to in our imminent future.

I'm not an energy expert and I'm bad with stats, but thanks to a knowledge database and community called The Great Simplification I've listened to hundreds such experts talk about what can be summed up as a scholarly discipline of energy realism.

Since Nate Hagens & friends have said all that needs to be said far more intelligently on this matter than I ever could, from here on out I asked the computer to "do my homework for me" by summarizing the TGS thesis into a few counter-points, manually edited for brevity and best-effort source verification.
New energy inputs aren't replacing anything, they're being added on top.

features.contentPlaintext: Our World in Data, global energy substitution
Energy Institute Statistical Review 2025

block.plaintext: Every energy transition in history has been additive, not subtractive — wood didn't go away when we found coal, coal didn't go away when we found oil*. The current one is no exception so far. The Energy Institute's 2025 Statistical Review found global energy demand and fossil consumption both hit all-time highs in 2024, with clean energy "layered on top of rising demand, not yet replacing conventional sources at scale"*.

features.contentPlaintext: Global Carbon Budget 2025

block.plaintext: Fossil CO₂ emissions hit a record 38.1 billion tonnes in 2025, up 1.1%, driven by growth in all three fossil fuels — coal +0.8%, oil +1%, gas +1.3%*.
Any "turbodeployment" we do today necessarily inreases our burn rate of fossil fuels.
No such thing as "free" energy.

Sunlight is free, capturing it is not. Solar panels, turbines, transmission, and the minerals, steel and concrete to mount them are manufactured, mined, and transported using — right now — a fossil-fuelled industrial base.

features.contentPlaintext: IEA, The Role of Critical Minerals in Clean Energy Transitions

block.plaintext: The honest term is rebuildables, not renewables: the hardware wears out in ~20–30 years and has to be rebuilt from a finite stock of source materials*.

features.contentPlaintext: same IEA report, executive summary

block.plaintext: A clean-energy economy is a more mineral-intensive economy — an EV needs roughly six times the mineral inputs of a conventional car, an onshore wind plant nine times a gas plant*.
Electricity is not energy.

features.contentPlaintext: IEA electricity statistics

block.plaintext: Solar overwhelmingly produces electricity, and electricity is only about a fifth of final energy use globally*.

features.contentPlaintext: IEA, Net Zero Roadmap

block.plaintext: The other ~80% — the heat to make steel and cement, the diesel in long-haul trucking and shipping, the feedstock for ammonia fertilizer that roughly half of humanity's food calories depend on — is still overwhelmingly molecules, not electrons, and far harder to electrify*. Decarbonizing the power sector is the easy fifth of the clean-energy transition.
Efficiency and abundance increase consumption.

features.contentPlaintext: Wikipedia: Jevons paradox

block.plaintext: Cheaper, more abundant energy doesn't lead to less throughput; historically it leads to more. That's Jevons' paradox, observed since 1865*.

features.contentPlaintext: IEA, Energy and AI

block.plaintext: The same AI that "does our homework" is now a material new load on the grid, with the IEA projecting data-centre electricity demand to more than double by 2030*.

features.contentPlaintext: Ember Q3 2025 Global Power Report
IEA World Energy Outlook 2025, via Carbon Brief

block.plaintext: The power sector may genuinely be near or already past 'peak oil'. Fossil power generation is projected to stay essentially flat in 2025 for the first time outside a pandemic, with renewables now meeting most demand growth*, and the IEA's stated-policies view still has total fossil use peaking before 2030*.
We can only go from 'flat' to 'declining' if we stop turbodeploying energy-eaters in lockstep with energy-producers.
The sun's energy is effectively infinite. Our ability to harvest, store, transport, and materialize it into the machine-work that powers civilization is very much not.

If you want the long-form version of this argument, the three best on-ramps are Nate Hagens' original Energy Blindness monologue, the Oil 101 series and his recent conversation with thermodynamicist Tad Patzek, (see the extensive bibliography for further reading).

value.title: Roomy basics

block.plaintext: So you've ended up in a Roomy space. It'll look something like this, though probably with just a single space icon in your left-most sidebar since you've just arrived.
The basics of Roomy are the the same as other group messaging apps like Discord or Slack; there are channels, you write posts in them and those posts can be replied or reacted to.
Images? Yes! Gifs? Not yet😿
You can also hover over a post and click on this icon..
that'll let you create a new thread from that post (moderators can string several posts together).
This is where Roomy and the likes of Discord diverge.
In Discord, threads are considered digressions; temporary sidebars with a limited time in the spotlight.
In Roomy, threads are how you put evergreen topics into the long-term memory of your community.

NOTE: When threadified your post will disappear from the channel feed and reappear in the sidebar with its given title. Like many things in Roomy alpha this isn't how we intend for it to work, it's just where it's at right now.
Every thread that's been created in any channel is aggregated and shown in the global Index of the space.

The real magic behind it all that we haven't got the UI to show off yet is that behind the scenes Roomy works very similarly to a git-like version-control system. Posts can be moved around losslessly while maintaining a clear record of provenance, from half-baked thought to polished article. Zeu presented this notion of message gardening at last year's ATmosphereConf, some half-dozen iterations ago.
This means that following the conclusion of this year's ATmosphereConf the moderators of the space will subsequently have the ability to curate the archives for optimal readability.
Known Issues
Being pre-eminently alpha software, there are a lot of things that don't yet work as intended in Roomy. Some of these include:

value.title: Redd demokratiet til prisen av et svømmebasseng

block.plaintext: Ti minutter fra hvor jeg bor i Oslo ligger det flotte Tøyenbadet som åpnet på starten av året. Jeg elsker dette bassenget; jeg ventet mange år på gjenåpningen etter at det ble revet og rekonstruert fra grunnen av.

Likevel, om jeg kunne tryllet dette bassenget bort for å få pengene tilbake, med all smerten det ville medført når tusenvis av folk, familier og smilende barn blir frarådet gledesrik mosjon og fellesskap, så hadde jeg gjort det.

Du skjønner, jeg måtte trylle vekk bassenget fordi det kostet 2 milliarder kroner å bygge, og akkurat nå, for prisen av et enkelt svømmebasseng i Norge, så kan vi styre det verdensomspennende demokratiske skipet vekk fra undergang i fascismens gap.

Her i Norge roer freden, men i realiteten er vi midt inne i en kald verdenskrig med rollene reversert: Tyskland og dets liberale allierte i Europa står opp mot et fascistisk USA som er innstilt på verdensherredømme, selv om det ikke vil være mye av verden igjen å herske over når støvet har lagt seg.
Og så langt er det USA som vinner fordi de allerede eier og driver hovedvekten av den digitale infrastrukturen vi alle har blitt avhengige av.
Europa Kan Ikke Forsvare Demokratiet på Amerikanske Servere.
In the short term, Europe needs home-grown social networks to cement political sovereignty.

I informasjonsalderen styrer den som eier kommunikasjonsmidlene også verden. Hver eneste autokrat og oligark på toppen av det globale hierarkiet har sørget for å eie enten et sosialt nettverk eller i det minste noen par aviser.
Bygg sammen med Europa
Det ligger enorm makt i kontroll over massemedier, og de mektigste har investert pengene sine deretter. Europa taper informasjonskrigen, og de vet det.

Jeg kommer nylig tilbake fra Eurosky eventet i Berlin, hvor teknologer og politikere møttes for å utveksle vår ekspertise og visjon for Europas digitale framtid, ment som en aksjonsdrevet oppfølger til Summit on European Digital Sovereignty dagen før.
Dette initiativet er EUs mest lovende satsing på suverenitet i sosiale medier, og utvikles som et kooperativt supplement til det USA-baserte Bluesky.
Det som gjør Bluesky annerledes enn alle de milliardær-eide plattformene, bortsett fra det faktum at det ikke eies av en milliardær, er at under Bluesky ligger en åpen nettverksprotokoll.

Det finnes mye spennende teknologi, men jeg er snevert fokusert på Bluesky og den underliggende teknologien fordi den troverdig truer USAs overherredømme nok til at den amerikanske staten aktivt bekjemper Bluesky inc. med både juridiske og sosiale midler.

block.plaintext: Mens Eurosky bygges opp kan vi allerede se en lignende trend i Canada hvor oppstarten Gander har så langt håvet inn over 10 millioner kroner direkte fra borgere som er lei av sin aggressive nabo i sør.

Som vanlig skuer Norge usikkert fra sidelinjen og venter på at krefter utenfor vår kontroll skal avgjøre vår skjebne. Det er her mine nyvunnede 2 milliarder kroner kommer inn i bildet; nå bygger vi NorSky! Men ikke alene og fra grunnen av slik vi måtte gjøre med Tøyenbadet.

Det fine med åpne protokoller og delt infrastruktur er at vi kan løse dette problemet slik Norge best vet hvordan: ved å kaste penger på det, omtrent slik andre oljestater i Midtøsten allerede har gjort med stor effekt. Med andre ord, vil vi forbli relevant i den digital verdensordenen må vi gjøre som Elon og kjøpe et sosialt nettverk.

Forskjellen er av vi investerer i verdensdemokratiet i stedet for den autoritære markedsstaten. Alt vi trenger å gjøre er å støtte Eurosky-prosjektet, som allerede har en visjon og et team på plass som er verdimessig på linje med våre nasjonale interesser.
Velkommen til moderne statskunst.
Et enkelt svømmebasseng er en triviell sum penger for et land med Norges enorme rikdom, og hver dag vi ikke klarer å effektivt bruke kapitalen vår er en strategisk fiasko av historiske proporsjoner.

Penger har vi. Det som mangler er politisk vilje og visjon. I det 21. århundre kan jeg ikke tenke meg noen bedre måte å beskytte landets suverenitet og våre barns sikkerhet på enn å investere tilstrekkelig i vårt folks digitale selvbestemmelse, før vår side i det digitale skillet blir bestemt på våre vegne av større makter.

value.title: Bluesky should take on Substack

block.plaintext: The mass migrations are over. When X/Twitter’s Mecha-Hitler doesn’t move people in droves it’s safe to assume that Bluesky has seen its last big wave of signups resulting from Elon’s continued transgressions.

As a member of Bluesky I personally don’t mind the slowed growth at all; 30-40 million people is more than enough for a lively discussion across borders and cultures, and the AT protocol network is bound to greatly expand long-term as its pluriverse of interoperable platforms matures.

The ones who do probably mind are the investors who wanna see the line go up asap, if not in revenue yet then at least in user numbers. Several months ago there was talk of Bluesky PBC soon-to-be-announcing another funding round, which hasn't yet materialized.
Conjecture aside, I think Bluesky has an obvious opportunity in front of it: Instead of competing with X/Twitter, compete with Substack:

content.plaintext: Unlike generic social media, newsletter subscriptions are actually a functional business model.
Bluesky as a network (~40m) is bigger than Substack's (est. 20-35m).
Substack ventured into microblogging with Notes; short- and long-form blogging work well together.
A fully functional MVP exists in Leaflet (more on that below).
Bluesky is already building their own payments platform, but there's no way they would be profitable on transaction fees alone: They need a flagship product.

block.plaintext: Substack has to be disrupted. Why? Because they don't mind funding Nazis and they'll exercise vendor lock-in whenever given the opportunity. The partial openness of their proprietary platform is merely an accidental side effect of how email newsletters inherently work.
Ghost and a handful other top-notch newsletter alternatives do already exist, but none have the network power of Bluesky.
Acquire Leaflet for fun and profit
Bluesky could make a pivot with minimal friction by amicably absorbing the excellent Leaflet.
Note: I've talked to the Leaflet developers on multiple occasions and I'm a fan of their work, but I did not discuss this post nor the hypothetical acquisition herein with them prior to publishing.

We should always be wary of platform consolidation, but this case presents a very natural coupling. Both projects are open source, based on atproto and use the React framework, so they're technologically aligned.
They're also mutually complementary business ventures:

content.plaintext: a bespoke payments network is essential to compete with incumbents on platform fees; Leaflet can't do that (easily) on their own.
a competitive publishing suite is a big lift only doable by a dedicated team; Bluesky can't do that (easily) on their own.

block.plaintext: Every smidge of information shared about Bluesky's business plan has been consistently vague, presumably because they don't have anything concrete yet. That's no surprise since mainstream social networks have never been profitable with any model other than ad-supported surveillance capitalism, which Bluesky is admirably trying to avoid.

So far they've also shied away from "eating up" any of the smaller fish in their still nascent ecosystem. While they're right to be very cautious to do so, I posit that they've been too restrained for their own good. The openness of Bluesky's platform has lead to a multitude of ventures rapidly exploring nearly every vertical imaginable, leaving very little left to play with for Bluesky PBC. But if the benevolent blue butterfly perishes, so do the rest of us.
(Sure the network is decentralized, but it's not yet sustainably distributed enough to absorb a blow of that magnitude.)

A highly resourced Substack alternative could be just the substantial revenue generator they need, putting them on a clear path to profitability and re-framing their pitch to prospective investors: When Bluesky is compared to Substack instead of X or Threads, Bluesky is already ahead in user acquisition!

value.description: Better to challenge an incumbent with a real business model.
